               I. Executive Summary

               1. Overview

                    1.1. Summary of Regulatory Action
               Ensartinib (ENSACOVE) is an oral inhibitor of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK), ROS proto-
               oncogene 1 (ROS1) and mesenchymal-epithelial transition (MET) kinases, among multiple other
               kinases. Gene rearrangements (fusions) in ALK have the potential to be oncogenic drivers and
               have been observed in a variety of tumor types, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
               Ensartinib is not currently FDA-approved for any indication.
               Xcovery Holdings Inc. (the Applicant) is seeking FDA approval of ensartinib for the treatment of
               adult patients with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC whose tumors are ALK-positive (b) (4)
                                                   (b) (4)




                    1.2. Conclusions on Substantial Evidence of
                        Effectiveness
               Substantial evidence of effectiveness (SEE) was established with one adequate and well-
               controlled clinical investigation and confirmatory evidence.
               The Applicant has provided SEE to support the traditional approval of ensartinib for the
               treatment of adult patients with locally advanced or metastatic ALK-positive NSCLC who have
               not previously received an ALK-inhibitor. The recommendation for traditional approval is based
               on the demonstration of an improvement in progression-free survival (PFS) observed in
               eXALT3, a multiregional, open-label, randomized study of ensartinib compared to crizotinib in
               patients with advanced NSCLC with an ALK rearrangement. Eligible patients were allowed to
               have up to one prior regimen of chemotherapy in the locally advanced or metastatic setting.
               Patients were randomized 1:1 to receive ensartinib 225 mg orally once daily (QD) or crizotinib
               250 mg orally twice daily (BID) on 28-day cycles until disease progression or unacceptable
               toxicity. Randomization was stratified by prior chemotherapy (0 versus 1), Eastern Cooperative
               Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (0/1 versus 2), presence of central nervous system
               (CNS) metastases (yes or no), and geographic regions (Asia versus the rest of the world). The
               main efficacy endpoint was PFS as evaluated by blinded independent central review (BICR)
               according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version (v.) 1.1. Key
               secondary efficacy endpoints were overall survival (OS), BICR-assessed CNS response rate,
               time to CNS progression, and overall response rate (ORR).
               The primary efficacy population included 290 patients who were randomized to either ensartinib
               (n=143) or crizotinib (n=147). The results of the primary analysis with a data cutoff (DCO) of
               July 1, 2020, demonstrated a PFS hazard ratio (HR) of 0.56 (95% CI: 0.40, 0.79; p-value
               0.0007). The median PFS was 25.8 months (95% CI: 21.8, not estimable (NE)) in the ensartinib
               arm and 12.7 months (95% CI: 9.2, 16.6) in the crizotinib arm. The point estimate for overall

                                   estimates that there will be 234,580 new cases of lung cancer
                                   in the United States in 2024 with approximately 125,070
                                   deaths (SEER Fact Sheets). Eighty-five percent of lung cancer
                                   cases are diagnosed at later stages, and for patients with
                                   distant metastasis, the 5-year survival rate is less 5.9 – 8.6%,

                                 • The estimated incidence of ALK rearrangements in NSCLC is
                                   approximately 5%. Clinical characteristics of patients with ALK
                                   rearrangements include adenocarcinoma histology and more
                                   likely to be never or light smokers (Riely, 2024). The overall
                                   survival for patients with ALK-positive NSCLC who have
                                   received contemporary therapy with a 2nd or 3rd generation
                                   ALK inhibitor is likely improved compared to patients without
                                   an actionable genomic alteration, but is not well-characterized;
                                   OS data at the time of the respective approvals was not
                                   mature. In the cases of the studies supporting approval of
                                   lorlatinib and alectinib, the median OS in the investigational
                                   arm has not been reached or has not been reported due to
                                   immaturity in subsequent published analyses {Solomon, 2023
                                   #31}{Mok, 2020 #32}. In the final analysis of PROFILE 1014, a
                                   randomized trial of crizotinib vs. chemotherapy as first-line
                                   treatment in patients with ALK positive non-squamous NSCLC,
                                   the median OS was not reached (NR) with crizotinib (95% CI:
                                   45.8 months, NR) and was 47.5 months with chemotherapy

                    2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
               Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer and cancer-related death in the United States, with 80-
               85% of all lung cancer cases classified as NSCLC. The American Cancer Society estimates that
               there will be 234,580 new cases of lung cancer in the United States in 2024 with
               approximately125,070 deaths, as indicated in SEER Fact Sheets (NCI 2024a). Eighty-five
               percent of lung cancer cases are diagnosed at later stages, and for patients with distant
               metastasis, the 5-year relative survival rate is approximately 5.9 – 8.6%, depending upon
               histology, as indicated by SEER data (NCI 2024b). The estimated incidence of ALK
               rearrangements in NSCLC is approximately 5%. Clinical characteristics of patients with ALK
               rearrangements include adenocarcinoma histology, and more likely to be never or light smokers
               (Riely et al. 2024). In addition, ALK-positive NSCLC carries a high risk of metastasis to the
               CNS with CNS metastases present in approximately 22-33% of patients with ALK-positive
               NSCLC at initial diagnosis (Aldea et al. 2020). The overall survival for patients with ALK-
               positive NSCLC who have received contemporary therapy with a 2nd or 3rd generation ALK
               inhibitor is likely improved compared to patients without an actionable genomic alteration, but is
               not well-characterized; OS data at the time of the respective approvals was not mature. In the
               cases of the studies supporting approval of lorlatinib and alectinib, the median OS in the
               investigational arm has not been reached or has not been reported due to immaturity in
               subsequent published analyses {Solomon, 2023 #31}{Mok, 2020 #32}(Solomon 2023, Mok
               2020). In the final analysis of PROFILE 1014, a randomized trial of crizotinib vs. chemotherapy
               as first-line treatment in patients with ALK positive non-squamous NSCLC, the median OS was
               not reached (NR) with crizotinib (95% CI: 45.8 months, NR) and 47.5 months with
               chemotherapy (95% CI: 32.2 months, NR). Survival probability at 4 years was 56.6% (95% CI:
               48.3%, 64.1%) with crizotinib and 49.1% (95% CI: 40.5%, 57.1%) with chemotherapy
               {Solomon, 2018 #33}. (Solomon, 2018)
               There are five other ALK inhibitors approved in the United States for the first-line treatment of
               metastatic ALK-positive NSCLC: alectinib, lorlatinib, ceritinib, crizotinib, and brigatinib.
               Crizotinib is a first generation ALK inhibitor that received accelerated approval (AA) in 2011 for
               the treatment of patients with previously treated ALK-positive NSCLC. In 2014, crizotinib
               received traditional approval for the treatment of metastatic ALK-positive NSCLC based on an
               improvement in median PFS (10.9 months for crizotinib compared to 7 months in patients who
               received platinum-based chemotherapy). The development of resistance mutations and brain
               metastases remains a significant factor in the rate of disease recurrence and the poor prognosis of
               this disease.
               Second and third-generation ALK tyrosine-kinase inhibitors (TKIs), including alectinib,
               lorlatinib, brigatinib, and ceritinib, have subsequently been approved. These have varying
               degrees of CNS penetrance and activity against ALK kinase inhibitor resistance mutations.
               Alectinib and lorlatinib were granted traditional approval for first-line ALK-positive metastatic
               NSCLC based on improvements in PFS over crizotinib. Second and third generation ALK
               inhibitors are SOC in the United States for the first-line treatment of metastatic ALK-positive
               NSCLC.
               The Applicant has provided SEE to support the traditional approval of ensartinib for the
               treatment of adult patients with ALK-positive locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC who have

               on the demonstration of an improvement in PFS observed in eXALT3, an open-label,
               multiregional, randomized study of ensartinib compared to crizotinib in patients with advanced
               NSCLC with an ALK rearrangement. Eligible patients were allowed to have up to one prior
               regimen of chemotherapy in the locally advanced or metastatic setting. Patients were randomized
               1:1 to receive ensartinib 225 mg orally QD or crizotinib 250 mg orally BID on 28-day cycles
               until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Randomization was stratified by prior
               chemotherapy (0 versus 1), ECOG performance status (0/1 versus 2), presence of CNS
               metastases (yes or no), and geographic regions (Asia versus the rest of the world). The main
               efficacy endpoint was PFS as evaluated by IRR according to RECIST v.1.1. Key secondary
               efficacy endpoints were OS, BICR-assessed CNS response rate, time to CNS progression, and
               ORR.
               The primary efficacy population included 290 patients who were randomized to either ensartinib
               (n=143) or crizotinib (n=147). The results of the primary analysis with a DCO of July 1, 2020,
               demonstrated a PFS HR of 0.56 (95% CI: 0.4, 0.79; p 0.0007). The median PFS was 25.8 months
               (95% CI: 22, NE) in the ensartinib arm and 12.7 months (95% CI: 9.2, 16.6) in the crizotinib
               arm. The point estimate for ORR was slightly higher in the ensartinib arm, with overlapping 95%
               CIs, with ORR 75% (95% CI: 66, 81) in the ensartinib arm compared to 67% (95% CI: 58, 74) in
               the crizotinib arm. The complete response rate was 12% in the ensartinib arm versus 5% in the
               crizotinib arm. The median duration of response (DOR) was not estimable (95% CI 22.0, NE) in
               the ensartinib arm and 27.3 months (95% CI 12.9, NE) in the crizotinib arm. At the time of the
               primary PFS analysis, OS results were immature. At the time of the final OS analysis (DCO
               September 14, 2023), the OS HR was 0.88 (95% CI: 0.63, 1.23; p 0.457).
               Providing additional support for the effectiveness of ensartinib, a prespecified analysis of CNS
               response rate (CNS ORR) by BICR in patients with baseline measurable CNS disease
               demonstrated a higher CNS ORR in the ensartinib arm (n=17) versus the crizotinib arm (n=24),
               with CNS ORR of 59% (95% CI 33, 82) and 21% (95% CI 7, 42), respectively.
               Supportive evidence for this approval includes ORR and DOR data from Study 101, an open-
               label, single-arm dose escalation and expansion study of ensartinib in patients with ALK-positive
               solid tumors conducted in the United States The confirmed ORR per RECIST v.1.1 as
               determined by investigator among 82 patients with ALK positive NSCLC who had received a
               prior ALK TKI was 28% (95% CI: 19%, 39%), with a median DOR of 8.2 months (95%CI: 5.5,
               12.0). The ORR in patients who had received prior crizotinib (n=41) was 46% (95%CI: 31, 63),
               with a median DOR of 8.2 months (95% CI: 5.6, 12.0). However, among 41 patients with ALK-
               positive NSCLC who had previously received a 2nd or 3rd generation ALK inhibitor (the SOC
               first-line therapy in the United States), the ORR was 10% (95% CI: 2.7%, 23%) with a median
               DOR of 7.9 months (95% CI: 3.9, NE). The results indicate that some patients with ALK-
               positive NSCLC previously treated with an ALK inhibitor may respond, particularly after
               receiving crizotinib as the first ALK inhibitor for metastatic disease, and provide supportive
               evidence of the antitumor activity of ensartinib in ALK-positive NSCLC. However, current
               SOC in the United States for treatment-naïve patients is treatment with a 2nd or 3rd generation
               ALK inhibitor, which has demonstrated improvement in PFS over crizotinib in randomized
               controlled trials. Therefore, only data for patients who have previously received a 2nd or 3rd
               generation ALK inhibitor are considered relevant to the U.S. SOC, and in this setting, there is
               insufficient data to support evidence of effectiveness of ensartinib for patients previously treated

               The observed safety profile of ensartinib is acceptable in the context of a life-threatening disease.
               The safety review focused on the 458 patients treated with ensartinib at the recommended phase
               2 dose in the pooled safety population, including data from the 143 patients treated with
               ensartinib in eXALT3. The most common (≥20%) treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs)
               due to any cause in patients (n=458) treated with ensartinib were rash, musculoskeletal pain,
               constipation, pruritus, cough, nausea, edema, vomiting, fatigue, and pyrexia. The most frequent
               Grade 3 or 4 laboratory abnormality (≥2%) were increased uric acid, decreased lymphocytes,
               increased alanine aminotransferase, decreased phosphate, increased gamma glutamyl transferase,
               increased magnesium, increased amylase, decreased sodium, increased glucose, decreased
               hemoglobin, increased bilirubin, decreased potassium, and increased creatine phosphor kinase.
               In eXALT3, serious adverse reactions occurred in 23% of patients treated with ensartinib.
               Serious adverse reactions that occurred in ≥1% were pneumonia (4.9%), hemorrhage (2.1%),
               rash (2.1%), and cellulitis (1.4%). One fatal adverse reaction (0.7%) occurred due to
               bronchopneumonia. Permanent discontinuation of ensartinib due to an adverse reaction occurred
               in 12% of patients. Adverse reactions which resulted in permanent discontinuation of ensartinib
               (≥1%) included increased blood bilirubin (1.4%), increased conjugated bilirubin (1.4%),
               increased ALT (2.1%), increased AST (2.1%), and pneumonitis/ILD (2.1%). The following key
               toxicities will be described in the Warnings and Precautions section of product labeling:
               interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, hepatotoxicity, dermatologic adverse reactions,
               bradycardia, hyperglycemia, visual disturbances, increased creatinine phosphokinase,
               hyperuricemia, embryofetal toxicity, and the potential for allergic reactions since the product
               contains tartrazine.
               The submitted evidence meets the statutory evidentiary standard for traditional approval. The
               observed improvement in PFS in eXALT3 is statistically robust and clinically meaningful. Based
               on the favorable risk-benefit assessment for this population with a serious, life-threatening
               disease, the submitted evidence supports traditional approval of ensartinib for the following
               indication:
               For the treatment of adult patients with ALK-positive locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC
               who have not previously received an ALK-inhibitor.

               5. Pharmacologic Activity, Pharmacokinetics,
                   and Clinical Pharmacology

                    5.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential
                        Effectiveness
               The nonclinical data support the potential effectiveness of ensartinib based on the following
               findings (see Section 13 for detailed reviews of these study reports).

               In Vitro Activity
               In an in vitro kinase screen, ensartinib inhibited ALK (IC50<0.25nM) and other kinases including
               c-MET (IC50=0.74nM) and ROS1 (IC50=10nM) at concentrations below those achievable at the
               recommended clinical dose of 225 mg ensartinib (free Cmax of approximately 39nM based on
               ~91.6% mean plasma protein binding in humans and a clinical Cmax of 292 ng/mL). A Cell Titer
               Blue proliferation assay demonstrated that ensartinib inhibited the in vitro proliferation of lung
               cancer cell lines bearing ALK fusion variants at clinically relevant concentrations. echinoderm
               microtubule associated protein-like 4 (EML4)-ALK fusions were used in several pharmacology
               studies. These fusion oncogenes contain an N terminus derived from EML4 and a C terminus
               containing the complete intracellular tyrosine kinase domain of ALK. Ensartinib inhibited H3122
               NSCLC cells expressing the EML4-ALK E13;A20 fusion variant with an IC50 of 15nM, and
               H2228 NSCLC cells expressing the EML4-ALK E6a/b;A20 fusion variant with an IC50 of 45nM.
               While Ba/F3 cells require interleukin-3 (IL-3) for viability, Ba/F3 cells stably expressing the
               EML4-ALK fusion are IL-3 independent. Ensartinib inhibited cell proliferation of Ba/F3 cells
               harboring wild type EML4-ALK with an IC50 of 22nM. Ensartinib also inhibited Ba/F3 cells
               harboring EML4-ALK fusions containing the secondary ALK mutations L1196M or C1156Y
               with IC50 values of 106nM and 48nM, respectively. As assessed by immunoblotting, ensartinib
               inhibited the phosphorylation of ALK and its downstream targets extracellular signal-regulated
               kinase (ERK), protein kinase B (AKT), and ribosomal protein S6 in lysates isolated from H3122
               EML4-ALK E13; A20 lung cancer cells.

               In Vivo Studies
               Ensartinib exhibited in vivo antitumor activity in an immunodeficient murine model of human
               NSCLC harboring EML4-ALK. Female nude mice injected subcutaneously with H3122 lung
               cancer cells harboring EML4-ALK E13/A20 received 0 or 25 mg/kg of ensartinib QD or
               25 mg/kg BID for 3 weeks via oral gavage. Ensartinib induced dose-dependent inhibition of
               tumor growth compared to controls, with BID treatment nearly completely inhibiting tumor

                    5.2. Clinical Pharmacology/Pharmacokinetics

                        5.2.1. Executive Summary
               The clinical pharmacology review of this NDA focused on the assessment of acceptance of the
               proposed ensartinib dosage administered without regard to food, dosage recommendations in
               patients with hepatic impairment, and dosing strategies for concomitant medications with
               potential drug-drug interactions (DDIs).
               The proposed dosage of ensartinib 225 mg orally QD without regard to food is acceptable for
               treatment of patients with ALK-positive NSCLC based on the following data: 1) antitumor
               activity of ensartinib were observed in dose cohorts of 150 – 250 mg QD and 200 - 250 mg QD
               in dose finding studies; 2) the clinical effectiveness of ensartinib 225 mg QD was demonstrated
               in the pivotal trial, Study X396-CLI-301, (See Section 6 for details) compared to crizotinib; 3)
               the overall safety and tolerability of ensartinib is acceptable and clinically manageable; 4)
               exposure-response (E-R) analysis for efficacy showed positive association between average daily
               area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) of ensartinib and primary endpoint, PFS; 5) E-R
               analysis for safety showed significant relationship between AUC at steady state and adverse
               events of special interest (AESIs) (all grade and Grade ≥3) and increase in alanine
               aminotransferase (ALT) / aspartate aminotransferase (AST); and 6) the food effect study, Study
               BTP-44313, showed that a high-fat meal did not have a clinically significant effect on ensartinib
               exposure supporting the recommendation of administering ensartinib without regard to food.
               Based on available data and E-R analyses for efficacy and safety, dosage recommendations
               include the following:
                    •   In patients with hepatic impairment (HI): no dosage adjustment is necessary in patients
                        with mild HI using National Cancer Institute Organ Dysfunction Working Group criteria.
                    •   Monitoring patients with moderate HI for increased adverse reactions and adjust dosage
                        as clinically indicated and avoiding use of ensartinib in patients with severe HI.
                    •   A post-marketing requirement (PMR) is needed to characterize ensartinib
                        pharmacokinetic (PK) in patients with moderate and severe HI to inform appropriate dose
                        adjustments.
               Dosing strategies for concomitant medications with potential DDIs include:
                    •   Avoid the concomitant use of ensartinib with strong or moderate CYP3A inhibitors and
                        inducers as ensartinib is extensively metabolized by CYP3A;
                    •   Avoid use of ensartinib with P-gp inhibitors as ensartinib is a substrate of P-gp.
                    •   Post-marketing clinical studies are required to assess the effect of a strong CYP3A
                        inhibitor and a P-gp inhibitor on the PK of ensartinib as a PMR and the effect of a strong
                        CYP3A inducer on the PK of ensartinib as a postmarketing commitment (PMC).

               The selection of 225 mg QD as the recommended phase 2 dose was based on an maximum
               tolerated dose (MTD) approach; as the clinical development of ensartinib started in 2012 and the
               phase 3 trial was fully accrued in 2018, the Applicant did not implement a dosage optimization
               strategy for dose selection. Given that insufficient clinical data and limited sample size are
               available at dose levels <200 mg and no integrated approach inclusive of PK, pharmacodynamic,
               dose-response or E-R relationship is available, whether a lower dose could provide clinically
               meaningful efficacy with less toxicity is not known.
               Nevertheless, a statistically significant improvement in the primary endpoint of PFS was
               observed in ensartinib arm at dosage of 225 mg QD compared to crizotinib control arm in the
               pivotal clinical trial, Study X396-CLI-301. Herein, the median PFS was about two times longer
               (approximately 26 months) in ensartinib arm than that in crizotinib arm (approximately 13
               months) with a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.56 (95% CI: [0.40, 0.79]; p-value 0.0007). Collectively,
               the proposed recommended dosage of 225 mg QD demonstrated a clinical meaningful efficacy in
               targeted patient population comparing to that of crizotinib. Dosage modifications for selected
               AEs are included in the approved labeling to manage adverse reactions.

                        6.2.1. Study 301/eXALT3

                            6.2.1.1. Design, Study 301/eXALT3
               Study eXALT3 is a randomized (1:1), open-label, global, active-controlled trial in patients with
               locally advanced (stage IIIB following prior chemotherapy or chemoradiation, or not amenable
               to chemoradiation) or metastatic ALK-positive NSCLC that have received up to one prior
               chemotherapy regimen and no prior treatment with an ALK TKI. Patients entered the trial
               following local testing and the protocol was later amended to include central testing using the
               FDA-approved Abbott Vysis fluorescence in situ hybridization assay. Randomization was
               stratified by prior chemotherapy (none versus 1 prior regimen), CNS metastases at baseline (yes
               versus no), ECOG (0 and 1 versus 2), and geographic region (Asia versus rest of the world).
               Patients received receive oral ensartinib 225 mg QD or crizotinib 250 mg BID on a 28-day
               schedule. Treatment continued until disease progression, unacceptable treatment-related toxicity,
               use of another anticancer therapy, or patient or physician decision to discontinue. Crossover was
               not allowed, but treatment beyond progression was allowed. The primary endpoint is PFS as

                            6.2.1.3. Statistical Analysis Plan, Study 301/eXALT3

               Efficacy Endpoints
               The primary efficacy endpoint was PFS as assessed by BICR (described by the Applicant as
               independent radiology review, or IRR) based on RECIST v.1.1 criteria. The key secondary
               endpoint was OS. Other secondary endpoints included BICR-assessed ORR, duration of
               response (DOR), CNS ORR and DOR for patients with CNS metastases at baseline. All efficacy
               analyses were conducted in the ITT Population.
               Censoring rules for PFS were defined as follows:
                    •   Patients last known to be alive and progression-free were to be censored at the date of the
                        last adequate objective disease assessment.
                    •   Patients with no on study disease assessments were to be censored at the date of
                        randomization unless death occurred prior to the first planned assessment (in which case
                        the death is an event).
                    •   Patients with inadequate baseline disease assessment were to be censored at the date of
                        randomization.
                    •   Patients who received alternate therapy prior to progression were to be censored at the
                        date of the last adequate objective assessment prior to receiving alternate therapy.
                    •   Patients who missed two or more consecutive objective disease assessments since the last
                        adequate response assessment and who have a PFS event (death or progression) after the
                        missing assessments and prior to a subsequent adequate objective assessment of non-
                        progression were to be censored at the time of last adequate objective assessment prior to
                        the missing assessments.
                    •   Patients who stop treatment for undocumented progression, toxicity, or reasons other than
                        documented progressive disease were to be censored at last adequate disease assessment.

               achieve 90% power to detect of a HR of 0.625 with a two-sided alpha of 0.05 in the ITT

               Efficacy Analyses
               PFS and OS were evaluated using the log-rank test without stratification in the ITT population. A
               log-rank test stratified by the randomization factors was used as supportive analysis. Kaplan-
               Meier method was used to estimate the survival distributions and medians and its 95%
               confidence intervals (CIs). HR was estimated using Cox proportional hazards model without
               stratification. A stratified Cox proportional hazards model with randomization factors was used
               as supportive analysis.

               Multiplicity Control
               The hierarchical testing procedure was used to control the overall Type I error rate at a two-sided
               level of 0.05. OS was eligible for testing at 0.05 only if PFS by BICR is statistically significant.
               Other secondary endpoints were not formally test and therefore were considered exploratory.

               Interim Analyses
               Two interim analyses of OS were planned at the time of the interim and final analysis of the
               primary endpoint of PFS, respectively. The O’Brien-Fleming Lan-DeMets alpha spending
               function was used to control for multiplicity due to analyses at multiple timepoints. The alpha
               spending for each interim analysis was updated based on the actual number of events observed at
               the time of analysis.

               Subgroup Analyses
               The primary analysis was performed on PFS by the prespecified subgroups including
               stratification factors (CNS metastases at baseline, prior chemotherapy, ECOG score, geographic

               observed for ensartinib over crizotinib across the majority of subgroups, except for patients over

               noteworthy that a smaller PFS benefit was observed for patients enrolled outside the Asia-Pacific

               was observed between the non-Asian and Asian subgroup. There is no compelling biologic

                        6.2.2. Study 101

                             6.2.2.1. Design, Study 101
               X396-CLI-101 (Study 101) is a first-in-human, open-label, dose-escalation and expansion study
               of ensartinib given as a single agent conducted in adult patients 18 years of age and older with
               advanced solid tumors; the expansion phase of the study enrolled patients with ALK-positive
               NSCLC. The study was conducted at 16 study centers in the United States.
               The objectives of the study were as follows:
               Primary:
                    •   To evaluate the safety/tolerability of X-396 (ensartinib) and determine the MTD of X-396
                        (ensartinib) as a single agent.
               Secondary:
                    •   To characterize the preliminary PK of X-396 (ensartinib) given as a single agent.
                    •   To explore the preliminary biological activity and clinical tumor response after treatment
                        with X-396 (ensartinib) given as a single agent.

                    6.3. Key Efficacy Review Issues

                        6.3.1. Are Results Applicable to the U.S. Population?
               Issue
               This application is supported primarily by the results of eXALT3 (Study 301), a multiregional
               randomized trial evaluating ensartinib versus crizotinib in patients with metastatic ALK-positive
               NSCLC, with 4% of patients enrolled in the United States. Based on randomized trials in patients
               with metastatic ALK-positive NSCLC for alectinib, lorlatinib and brigatinib demonstrating
               improvement in PFS compared to patients treated with crizotinib, the SOC treatment for patients
               with metastatic ALK-positive NSCLC who have not previously received an ALK inhibitor is
               currently a 2nd or 3rd generation ALK inhibitor. Given the limited enrollment of U.S. patients in
               the pivotal trial and questionable relevance of the comparator arm of crizotinib to current SOC,
               FDA considered whether the results of eXALT3 were relevant to the U.S. population.

               Background
               Per the U.S. Code of Federal Regulations, Section 21 314.106 (b), foreign data may be used as
               the sole basis for marketing approval if it meets the following criteria:
               1. The foreign data are applicable to the U.S. population and U.S. medical practice.
               2. The studies have been performed by clinical investigators of recognized competence.
               3. The FDA is able to validate the data through an onsite inspection or other appropriate means.

               initially evaluated investigational ALK inhibitors in comparison to chemotherapy (i.e., trials for

               investigational ALK inhibitors in comparison to crizotinib, and improvements in PFS with these
               products observed in these trials led to the traditional approval of these products (alectinib in
               2017, brigatinib in 2020, and lorlatinib in 2021).

               Assessment
               FDA considered several factors in assessing relevance to the U.S. population, including the
               extent of U.S. experience, demographics of patients enrolled in pivotal and supportive trials, and
               primary and supportive analyses of safety and efficacy. The Applicant provided documentation
               on the extent of the U.S. experience with ensartinib in clinical trials. The cumulative U.S.-based
               clinical experience includes the treatment of 185 patients, with 131 patients enrolled in the
               United States phase 1/2 Study X396-CLI-101; 14 of these patients were treatment-naïve patients
               with ALK-positive NSCLC (similar to the population enrolled in eXALT3). As previously
               stated, a small number (n=12) of U.S. patients were enrolled in eXALT3. The Applicant

               In considering the baseline and demographic characteristics of patients enrolled in eXALT3,
               FDA assessed that several racial or ethnic subgroups were underrepresented compared to the
               expected incidence in the U.S. population. For example, in the pooled safety population, only
               0.9% of patients were Black (and only 2 Black patients were treated on eXALT3, both in the
               control arm). According to a recent meta-analysis, there is a lower incidence of ALK fusions in
               Black patients versus other races, with 1% (95% CI, 0 to 2) prevalence in Black patients, 2%
               (95% CI, 1 to 3) in White patients, 7% (95% CI, 2 to 23) in Hispanic patients, and 6% (95% CI,
               1 to 11) in Asian patients (Costa et al. 2021). Hispanic or Latino patients comprised 4.8% of
               patients enrolled in the crizotinib arm and 10% of patients enrolled in the ensartinib arm in
               eXALT3.
               Studies 101 and eXALT3 were conducted under IND and discussed with FDA in several
               meetings (refer to Section 12). Studies BTP-28311 and BTP-42322 were conducted by Betta
               Pharmaceuticals, Inc. in China, and were not conducted under the U.S. IND. Studies BTP-28311
               and BTP-42322 were not reported in International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) format.
               Therefore, to demonstrate good clinical practice (GCP) compliance, each clinical study report
               was adapted as described in Guidance for Industry and FDA Staff, FDA Acceptance of Foreign
               Clinical Studies Not Conducted Under an IND Frequently Asked Questions, (March 2012).
               These studies were used as part of the pooled safety population and did not contribute directly to
               an assessment of efficacy.

               Conclusion
               FDA considered that the design of eXALT3, including the choice of comparator arm, was
               appropriate at the time of study conduct. The study was broadly multiregional and conducted
               under IND. Although several racial or ethnic groups were underrepresented in eXALT and in the
               pooled safety population, additional data will be requested as a post-marketing commitment to
               further understanding of the safety and effectiveness of ensartinib in underrepresented
               populations, as well as in older adults. Therefore, FDA considers the results of eXALT3 to be
               applicable to the U.S. population.

               consistency of treatment effect across subgroups to support the proposed indication. Although
               consistent results were observed across most subgroups suggesting an improvement in PFS and
               OS in patients treated with ensartinib compared to those treated with crizotinib, heterogenous
               results were observed across several subgroups, particularly across subgroups by gender, age,

               Background
               In FDA Guidance for industry, Clinical Studies Section of Labeling for Human Prescription
               Drug and Biological Products — Content and Format (January 2006), under 21 CFR
               314.50(d)(5)(v), effectiveness data must be presented by age, gender, and racial subgroups, in
               order to investigate the potential heterogeneity of treatment effects across subgroups, including
               the prespecified clinically important subgroups.
               In Study 301, there was a statistically significant PFS benefit of ensartinib over crizotinib in the
               overall population. However, the PFS HR was 0.48 (95% CI: 0.33, 0.70) for patients <65 years
               of age compared to 1.20 (95% CI: 0.51, 2.86) for patients ≥65 years of age. The PFS HR was
               0.34 (95% CI: 0.21, 0.57) for patients enrolled in Asia-Pacific region compared to 0.88 (95% CI:
               0.54, 1.41) for patients enrolled in rest of the world.
               There was no statistically significant evidence of OS benefit in the overall study population.
               Furthermore, OS results appeared to differ by gender and region of enrollment. The OS HR was
               1.22 (95% CI: 0.75, 1.99) for female patients compared to 0.65 (95% CI: 0.41, 1.02) for male
               patients. OS HR was 0.73 (95% CI: 0.46, 1.15) for patients enrolled in Asia-Pacific region
               compared to 1.08 (95% CI: 0.66, 1.76) for patients enrolled in rest of the world.
               FDA did not identify differences in pharmacokinetics or other biologic rationale to explain the
               observed differences by gender and region; therefore, these subgroup results were considered
               hypothesis generating rather than providing conclusive evidence of lack of efficacy within the
               subgroups.
               FDA also considered the consistency of treatment effect in patients with locally advanced
               disease (Stage IIIB following chemotherapy or chemoradiation or who were not candidates for
               chemoradiation), who represented 8% of the study population in eXALT3. The median PFS was
               NE in stage IIIB patients receiving ensartinib (95% CI: 11.8, NE) versus 29.1 months (95% CI:
               11.0, NE) for patients receiving crizotinib, with a slightly higher rate of progression (23% versus
               20%) in ensartinib arm. The median OS was 41.3 months in the ensartinib arm (95% CI: 24.5,
               NE) versus NE (28.1, NE). There was a higher rate of deaths (23% versus 10%) in the ensartinib
               arm versus the crizotinib arm. ORR was 100% for both arms.

               Assessment
               In response to FDA’s request regarding the interpretation of these inconsistencies in the
               subgroup analyses, the Applicant suggested that there could be potential confounding factors
               related to demographics. For example, female patients in the ensartinib arm included more
               current and former smokers compared to those in the crizotinib arm (28% versus 10%). The
               Applicant indicated that smoking status has been identified as a negative prognostic factor in
               other ALK TKI studies. Additionally, there was an imbalance in the utilization of subsequent
               therapy within the female subgroup, with female patients in the ensartinib arm utilizing fewer
               subsequent therapies compared to those in crizotinib arm (41% versus 76%).
               As the relatively limited numbers of events/patients within a subgroup (e.g., 53 patients ≥65
               years of age across both arms) make it difficult to assess treatment effect with adequate precision

                        7.1.2. Target Organs of Toxicity
               In the 13-week GLP-compliant toxicology studies, ensartinib was administered QD via oral
               gavage to rats (12.5, 25, or 50 mg/kg) and dogs (5, 10, or 20/15 mg/kg). The major target organ
               in both species was the skin. Rats exhibited skin scabbing that correlated microscopically with
               reversible hyperkeratosis and mixed cell inflammation. At exposures approximately equal to the
               clinical exposure based on AUC at 225 mg/day, dogs exhibited severe skin lesions particularly
               on the ear, which led to dose reduction. Ensartinib also distributed to the skin in an in vivo PK
               study in rats. Consistent with nonclinical findings, rash and pruritus were observed clinically
               with ensartinib, and the ensartinib label includes a warning for skin reactions.
               Another consistent finding between nonclinical and clinical studies included elevated liver
               enzymes. Ensartinib increased mean ALT and AST) in rats and dogs, which did not correlate
               with histologic findings in rats. Two high-dose female dogs exhibited elevated gamma-glutamyl
               transferase (GGT), which correlated histologically with moderate to marked hepatocellular
               vacuolation in the liver. Increased ALT, AST, and/or bilirubin have been reported clinically with
               ensartinib, and the ensartinib label includes a warning for hepatotoxicity. Additional target
               organs of toxicity in rats and/or dogs included the stomach, spleen, bone marrow, and lungs.

                        7.1.3. Reproductive and Developmental Toxicology
               Based on findings from EFD studies and its mechanism of action, Ensartinib can cause fetal
               harm when administered to a pregnant woman. The EFD study in rats showed that QD oral
               ensartinib administration to pregnant rats during the period of organogenesis resulted in
               increased embryo-fetal mortality, alterations to growth, and structural abnormalities in fetuses.
               Adverse embryo-fetal findings were seen at exposures approximately equivalent to the clinical
               exposure at the recommended dose of 225 mg/day based on AUC. The pharmacology/
               toxicology team therefore recommends a warning in the ensartinib label for embryo-fetal
               toxicity. Given that ensartinib is not genotoxic and has a half-life of approximately 30 hours,
               FDA recommends advising males and females of reproductive potential to use effective
               contraception during treatment with ensartinib and for 1 week after the last dose. See Sections
               8.4 and 13 for additional details.

                        7.1.4. Genetic Toxicology
               Ensartinib was not mutagenic in an in vitro Ames assay. Ensartinib induced a greater number of
               polyploid lymphocytes in an in vitro human lymphocyte chromosome aberration assay at
               concentrations as low as 1.8 µg/mL (~2.8µM; approximately 72 times the free human Cmax of
               39nM at the recommended dose of 225 mg/day), but was not clastogenic or aneugenic in vitro.
               Polyploidy alone does not indicate aneugenic potential and can result from cell cycle
               perturbations/delays or cytotoxicity (Muehlbauer et al. 2008). Further, ensartinib did not increase
               micronuclei in an in vivo rat bone marrow micronucleus assay. Based on the totality of data,
               ensartinib is not genotoxic.


                    7.2. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on
                        Drug Class or Other Drug-Specific Factors
               At the time of this review, five ALK inhibitors are approved for use in the United States:
               alectinib, brigatinib, ceritinib, crizotinib, and lorlatinib. Hepatotoxicity and interstitial lung
               disease have been observed with all approved products; however, other toxicities vary by
               product. Warnings included in the product label for other approved ALK inhibitors include
               photosensitivity, bradycardia, visual disturbances or vision disorders, severe myalgia with
               creatine phosphokinase increase, hemolytic anemia, hypertension, pancreatic enzyme elevation
               or pancreatitis, CNS effects, hyperglycemia, QT prolongation, renal impairment, hyperlipidemia,
               and gastrointestinal toxicity. Embryofetal toxicity is also included as a warning in the product
               label for all approved products.

                    7.4. FDA Approach to the Safety Review
               The clinical safety assessment of ensartinib is based primarily on data from patients enrolled in
               Study 301(eXALT3) (143 who received ensartinib and 147 who received crizotinib) and patients
               in the pooled safety population who received the recommended dose of ensartinib (n=458) with a
               safety DCO of July 1, 2020. FDA assessments in this review will refer to the recommended dose
               as 225 mg QD, as this is the dose that will be included in the United States Prescribing
               Information (USPI). The safety review of eXALT3 included review and analysis of the clinical
               study report, the Applicant’s risk: benefit assessment, case report forms, selected narratives, the
               integrated summary of safety (ISS), and the primary datasets submitted by the Applicant. The
               reviewers analyzed key safety datasets using several safety analysis queries with preferred terms
               and Grouped Terms. The FDA Safety Analysis Team provided support in conducting the safety
               analysis. The analysis of adverse events data were based on treatment-emergent adverse events
               (TEAEs) only, defined as AEs which emerged or worsened during the on-treatment period. The
               overall on-treatment period was defined from the first dose (Day 1) of ensartinib, up to and
               including 30 days after the last dose of study treatment, or death, whichever occurred earlier.
               Deaths were captured as part of the survival follow-up after the 30-day period following the last
               dose.
               In the original application submission, the Applicant provided datasets for the ISS and eXALT3
               populations with a safety DCO of July 1, 2020. Although eXALT3 collected data beyond this
               date, datasets containing data reflecting the April 1, 2023, DCO were not provided; results of
               safety analyses using this DCO were described in the application. FDA reviewed topline safety
               data using the later DCO and compared to results according to the July 1, 2020, DCO. As only
               data for eXALT3 was available after the July 1, 2020, DCO, any differences observed between
               the analyses according to different DCOs were most pronounced in results for the eXALT3 study
               population, and differences were smaller when comparing analyses for different DCOs using the
               ISS population. An overview of treatment-emergent adverse events in eXALT3 according to the
               2020 and 2023 DCOs is provided in Table 104. Differences observed based on the different
               DCOs were generally small. Notably, there were no new fatal treatment-emergent adverse events
               or serious adverse events which occurred in > 2% of patients based on the later DCO. Therefore,
               FDA relied upon analyses conducted using the originally submitted safety datasets with the July
               1, 2020 DCO.
               The safety data were collected at regular intervals and in accordance with best clinical practice
               for the patient population under study. The safety analyses supporting this application included
               all grades and Grade ≥3 all-causality and TEAEs, TEAEs leading to permanent discontinuation,
               temporary discontinuation, or dose modifications, serious TEAEs, and deaths. Analyses of
               hematology and biochemistry parameters, vital signs and electrocardiogram were also
               performed. Identified risks, potential risks and AEs of clinical interest were analyzed and
               described.
               Subgroup analyses were performed as necessary to further characterize the safety profile of
               ensartinib including the AESI. Adverse events occurring in patient treated with ensartinib from
               eXALT3 were compared to those occurring in the population treated with crizotinib and pooled
               population of ensartinib at the recommended dose (225 mg QD) in NSCLC (n=458, of which
               143 patients were from eXALT3).

                    7.5. Adequacy of the Clinical Safety Database
               The safety review approach described above is appropriate to allow for an adequate assessment
               of safety to inform the risk-benefit assessment for this NDA. The pooled safety population, used
               to inform Section 5 of labeling, included 458 patients with solid tumors. The pooled safety
               population reflects patents from eXALT3 Study (n=143), Study 101(n=98), Study BTP-28311
               (n=35), and Study BTP-42322 (n=182); data from this pooled population informs Section 5 of
               the USPI. Among the pooled safety population, there were 143 patients with metastatic NSCLC
               harboring ALK rearrangements enrolled in Study eXALT3; data from this subpopulation was
               used to inform Section 6 of the USPI.
               Notably, data collected for eXALT3 did not include collection of any laboratory evaluations for
               tests that were not specified in the study calendar. For example, creatine phosphokinase (CPK)
               was not specified in the study calendar; when investigators performed CPK testing, the data were
               not recorded in the study database unless the resulting laboratory abnormality was reported as an
               adverse event. However, all laboratory abnormalities for tests specified in the study calendar,
               even if performed off-schedule, were collected in the database. FDA typically observes that not
               all laboratory abnormalities are reported as adverse events, and thus that analyses of the
               laboratory dataset are more accurate for laboratory-based adverse events. FDA considered that
               the data from eXALT3 was sufficient to allow a safety review, but results should be interpreted
               in light of this limitation in data collection.

               hemorrhage and 1.1% of those patients experiencing a Grade 3 – 4 adverse event. This analysis

               represented in the pooled safety population included hemoptysis, intracranial hemorrhage,
               gastrointestinal hemorrhage, hematuria, upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, vaginal hemorrhage,

               assess a potential contribution of ensartinib. These events included 7 patients who experienced
               Grade 3 – 4 hemorrhage. Additionally, 3 patients had an SAE of hemorrhage (hemoptysis,
               disseminated intravascular coagulation, and intracranial hemorrhage) that required
               hospitalization. The Applicant noted that there was no evidence of bleeding or hemorrhage in
               nonclinical studies.

               patients treated with ensartinib had increased ALT, including 5% Grade 3. Increased AST
               occurred in 58% of patients treated with ensartinib, including 1.8% Grade 3. Increased bilirubin
               occurred in 12% of patients treated with ensartinib, including 2.3% Grade 3 and 0.2% Grade 4.
               There was one adverse event with preferred term of drug-induced liver injury; there were no
               cases that met criteria for Hy’s law in the pooled safety population.
               The median time to first onset of increased ALT or AST was 5.3 weeks (range: 0.4 weeks to 152
               weeks). Increased ALT or AST leading to dose interruption occurred in 4.6%; increased AST or
               ALT leading to dose reduction occurred in 2.6% of patients, and permanent discontinuation of
               ensartinib in 1.1% of patients. Increased bilirubin leading to dose interruption occurred in 1.3%;
               increased bilirubin leading to dose reduction occurred in 0.7% and permanent discontinuation of
               ensartinib in 1.3% of patients.

                            7.6.1.9. Adverse Events of Special Interest
               The eXALT3 protocol defined three items as “protocol-defined events of special interest:” 1)
               pregnancy, abortion, birth defects/congenital abnormalities, 2) any clinically significant
               electrocardiogram abnormalities and 3) study drug overdose. This section will address FDA’s
               evaluation of adverse events of special interest (AESIs), defined as significant identified or
               suspected adverse reactions with ensartinib, based on clinical data or other drugs in class, that are
               not discussed elsewhere in the review.

               Interstitial Lung Disease/Pneumonitis
               Ensartinib can cause severe ILD/pneumonitis. In the pooled safety population, ILD/pneumonitis
               occurred in 5% of patients, including Grade 3 in 1.3% and Grade 4 in 0.4%. No fatal cases with
               preferred terms ILD and pneumonitis were identified; narratives for fatal respiratory events (i.e.,
               dyspnea) were also reviewed for the potential to represent additional cases of pneumonitis, and
               the review team did not identify suspected cases. In eXALT3, 1.4% of patients receiving
               crizotinib experienced pneumonitis compared to 4.2% of patients treated with ensartinib.
               In the pooled safety population, ILD/pneumonitis leading to dose interruption occurred in 0.4%
               and permanent discontinuation of ensartinib in 1.5% of patients. ILD/pneumonitis will be
               included as a Warning and Precaution in the product label.

                Hepatotoxicity
               Refer to Section 7.6.1.7. Hepatoxicity will be included as a Warning and Precaution in the
               product label.

               Dermatologic Adverse Reactions
               Dermatologic adverse reactions were an identified safety risk in studies of ensartinib and
               proposed by the Applicant as a Warning and Precaution in the product label. Dermatologic
               adverse reactions included drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS),
               rash, pruritus, and photosensitivity.
               In the pooled safety population, dermatologic adverse reactions occurred in 80% of patients,
               including Grade 3 in 14% of patients. Rash (grouped term, refer to Table 33) occurred in 72% of
               patients, including Grade 3 in 12% of patients. The median time to onset of rash was 9 days
               (range: 1 day to 17.3 months). Pruritus occurred in 32% of patients with Grade 3 in 2.4%. There
               was one Grade 3 case of DRESS (0.2%).
               Ensartinib was interrupted in 12% of patients for dermatologic adverse reactions. Dermatologic
               adverse reactions leading to dose reduction occurred in 11% and permanent discontinuation of in
               1.5% of patients. In the pooled safety population, photosensitivity occurred in 0.9% of patients
               receiving ensartinib; all were Grade 1.
               Dermatologic adverse reactions will be described as a Warning and Precaution in the product
               label.

               Bradycardia
               Bradycardia was an identified safety risk in studies of ensartinib and proposed by the Applicant
               as a Warning and Precaution in the product label. Bradycardia is also an identified safety risk
               with other products in the same drug class.
               In the pooled safety population, bradycardia (heart rate less than 60 beats per minute) occurred in
               6% of patients. All bradycardia events were Grade 1 or 2. Bradycardia requiring dose reduction
               occurred in 0.2% and led to dose interruption in 0.4% of patients.

               Hyperglycemia
               FDA identified the risk of hyperglycemia in patients receiving ensartinib. In eXALT3, 49% of
               patients receiving ensartinib developed hyperglycemia, with 5% Grade 3 – 4; in the crizotinib
               arm, 35% of patients developed hyperglycemia, with 0.7% Grade 3 – 4 events. Given the
               increased risk compared to the crizotinib arm, including for Grade 3 – 4 events, FDA considered
               hyperglycemia to be contributed to by ensartinib; further, given the need to monitor and initiate
               specific treatment for hyperglycemia, a Warning and Precaution in the product label was
               considered necessary to enable the safe use of ensartinib.
               In the pooled safety population, based on laboratory data, 44% of patients receiving ensartinib
               experienced increased blood glucose, including Grade 3 in 2.5%. The median time to onset of
               increased blood glucose was 5.9 weeks (0.4 weeks to 3.4 years).

               Visual Disturbances
               Visual disturbances were an identified safety risk with ensartinib and proposed by the Applicant
               as a Warning and Precaution in the product label. Ensartinib can cause visual disturbances
               including blurred vision, diplopia, photopsia, vitreous floaters, visual impairment, visual field
               defect, and reduced visual acuity.
               In the pooled safety population, 8% of patients receiving ensartinib experienced visual
               disturbance, including 0.2% Grade 3. Visual disturbances led to dose interruption in 0.4% of
               patients. No patients permanently discontinued ensartinib due to visual disturbances.

               Hyperuricemia
               In the pooled safety population, based on adverse reactions, 6% of patients experienced
               hyperuricemia, with 0.4% Grade 3 and 0.7% Grade 4. Based on laboratory abnormality data in
               eXALT3, 39% of patients in Study 301 had hyperuricemia (all Grade 3-4) versus 27% of patients
               receiving crizotinib (also all Grade 3 – 4). Grade 3 based on the Common Terminology Criteria
               for Adverse Events, v 4.03 is defined as greater than the upper limit of normal to 10 mg/dL with
               physiologic consequences; the presence of physiologic consequences differentiates this from
               Grade 1 (there is no Grade 2 definition). In the pooled safety population, nine patients (1.9%)
               required hydration and two patients (0.4%) required urate-lowering medication.
               There were no reported cases of tumor lysis syndrome in the safety population. At FDA’s
               request, the Applicant performed an analysis using a case definition of tumor lysis syndrome
               (TLS) to evaluate for presence of hyperuricemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperkalemia and
               hypocalcemia; to align as closely as possible with the Cairo-Bishop definition of TLS (within 3
               days before or up to 7 days after initiation of therapy), the analysis was performed using

               Evaluation of increases in CPK were limited by the lack of standardized collection of laboratory
               data for CPK increase in eXALT3, since CPK was not specified as a laboratory evaluation to be
               performed at scheduled time points in the study protocol.

               laboratory data available, increased CPK occurred in 43% of patients who received ensartinib.
               The incidence of Grade 3 increased CPK was 1.5% and 0.5% were Grade 4. The median time to
               onset of increased CPK was 123 days (range: 3 days to 22 months). Increased CPK leading to
               dose interruption occurred in 0.2%, and dose reduction in 0.4%.

               adverse event. One event (0.7%) was Grade 4, and the remainder were Grade 1 or 2.

               with a similar mechanism of action, including hemolytic anemia, hypertension, pancreatitis, CNS

               4.2% of patients treated with ensartinib in eXALT3, compared to 2.1% of patients treated with
               crizotinib; in the pooled safety population 2.4% of patients experienced hypertension (0.7%
               Grade 3).

               2.7% treated with crizotinib; no Grade 3 events were reported in either arm.
               Increased triglycerides occurred in 15% of patients in the ISS, with 1% Grade 3 increases based
               on laboratory analyses; this analysis is limited by the lack of collection of laboratory data on
               serum triglycerides in eXALT3. Based on adverse events, 3.4% of patients in the crizotinib arm
               and 0.7% of patients in the ensartinib arm experienced hypertriglyceridemia in eXALT3.
               The product label for crizotinib describes a Warning and Precaution for gastrointestinal toxicity
               in pediatric and young adult patients with anaplastic large cell lymphoma or pediatric patients
               with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor. In eXALT3, patients in the crizotinib arm experienced
               higher rates of diarrhea (32% vs. 7% in the ensartinib arm), nausea (30% vs. 28% in the
               ensartinib arm), and vomiting (32% vs. 16% in the ensartinib arm). Constipation was more
               frequent in the ensartinib arm (31% vs. 26% in the crizotinib arm).
               Acute kidney injury (evaluated as a grouped term) occurred in 4.4% of patients in the ISS, with
               0.4% Grade 3. In eXALT3, 2.7% of patients in the crizotinib arm and 4.2% of patients in the
               ensartinib arm experienced acute kidney injury.
               Review of relevant adverse event data and associated laboratory abnormalities for these issues in
               the NDA submission did not indicate safety signals that rose to the level of inclusion as a
               Warning and Precaution in the product label.

               Background
               FDA’s review of safety evaluated data from patients enrolled in Study 301(eXALT3) (143 who
               received ensartinib and 147 who received crizotinib) and patients in the pooled safety population
               who received the recommended dose of ensartinib (n=458). In this pooled safety population, the
               most common adverse reactions (≥20%) were rash, musculoskeletal pain, constipation, pruritus,
               cough, nausea, edema, vomiting, fatigue, and pyrexia. The most frequent Grade 3 or 4 laboratory
               abnormalities (≥2%) were increased uric acid, decreased lymphocytes, increased alanine
               aminotransferase, decreased phosphate, increased gamma glutamyl transferase, increased
               magnesium, increased amylase, decreased sodium, increased glucose, decreased hemoglobin,
               increased bilirubin, decreased potassium, and increased creatine phosphokinase.
               In eXALT3, serious adverse reactions occurred in 23% of patients treated with ensartinib.
               Serious adverse reactions that occurred in ≥1% were pneumonia (4.9%), hemorrhage (2.1%),
               rash (2.1%) and cellulitis (1.4%). One fatal adverse reaction (0.7%) occurred due to
               bronchopneumonia. Permanent discontinuation of ensartinib due to an adverse reaction occurred
               in 12% of patients. Adverse reactions which resulted in permanent discontinuation of ensartinib
               (≥1%) included increased ALT (2.1%), increased AST (2.1%), pneumonitis/ILD (2.1%).
               increased blood bilirubin (1.4%), and increased conjugated bilirubin (1.4%),
               Dose interruptions of ensartinib due to an adverse reaction occurred in 41% of patients. Adverse
               reactions which required dose interruptions (≥2%) included rash (13%), increased ALT (6%),
               pneumonia (3.5%), edema (2.8%), pruritus (2.8%), pyrexia (2.8%), increased AST (2.1%),
               hemorrhage (2.1%), and decreased appetite (2.1%).
               Dose reductions of ensartinib due to an adverse reaction occurred in 24% of patients. Adverse
               reactions which required dose reductions (≥2%) included rash (11%), increased ALT (4.2%),
               pruritus (2.8%), and edema (2.1%).
               The review identified several key safety issues, including interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis,
               hepatotoxicity, dermatologic adverse reactions, bradycardia, hyperglycemia, visual disturbances,
               increased creatinine phosphokinase, hyperuricemia, and embryofetal toxicity. In addition, the
               product contains tartrazine, which may cause allergic reactions (though this was not a safety
               signal identified in the safety review).

               Assessment
               The review team considered the safety profile of ensartinib to be acceptable when assessed in the
               context of a life-threatening disease. In addition, although ensartinib can cause serious and
               severe toxicities, the safety concerns are described in product labeling. The following key
               toxicities will be described in the Warnings and Precautions section of product labeling:
               interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, hepatotoxicity, dermatologic adverse reactions,
               bradycardia, hyperglycemia, visual disturbances, increased creatinine phosphokinase,
               hyperuricemia, embryofetal toxicity, and the potential for allergic reactions since the product
               contains tartrazine. Ensartinib will be prescribed by oncologists who are trained to monitor and
               treat serious treatment-related toxicities. There were no significant safety concerns identified
               during the NDA review requiring additional risk management tools such as a Risk Evaluation
               and Mitigation Strategy.

                    8.2. Extrinsic Factors
               Drug-Drug Interactions
               FDA agrees with the Applicant’s proposed labeling recommendation to avoid concomitant use of
               ensartinib with strong or moderate CYP3A inhibitors and inducers. In addition, FDA
               recommends avoiding concomitant use of ensartinib with P-gp inhibitors. FDA considered the
               Applicant proposed post-marketing DDI study with acid reducing agents is unnecessary given
               the available in vitro solubility data and clinical PK and safety data of ensartinib in patients
               received concomitant mediations of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are sufficient to address this
               DDI. FDA’s rationale and supportive data for the above recommendations and determination are
               summarized below.

               Strong and Moderate CYP3A4 Inhibitors and P-gp Inhibitors
               In vitro studies showed that ensartinib is primarily metabolized by CYP3A and ensartinib is also
               a substrate of P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporter. Concomitant medications that are strong
               CYP3A inhibitors and/or P-gp inhibitors may increase the systemic exposure of ensartinib
               leading to potential increase in the incidence of adverse events. The Applicant did not conduct
               any clinical DDI study to characterize the effect of coadministration of a strong CYP3A inhibitor
               and a P-gp inhibitor with ensartinib on its PK, and safety. A post-marketing clinical DDI study is
               required to evaluate the effect of a strong CYP3A inhibitor and a P-gp inhibitor on the PK of
               ensartinib to inform appropriate dose recommendations when they are concomitantly used. In
               particular, the dose of ensartinib should be lower than 225 mg to accommodate the potential
               increase in ensartinib exposure. Additional DDI studies may be warranted pending on the results
               of the forementioned DDI study to evaluate the contribution from a strong CYP3A inhibitor and
               a P-gp inhibitor separately.

               Strong and Moderate CYP3A4 Inducers
               Given the metabolism of ensartinib was primarily mediated by CYP3A in vitro, concomitant
               medications that are strong CYP3A inducers may decrease the systemic exposure of ensartinib,
               thus compromise the antitumor activity of ensartinib. The Applicant did not conduct any clinical
               DDI study to characterize the effect of coadministration of a strong CYP3A inducer with
               ensartinib on its PK and efficacy. A post-marketing clinical DDI study is recommended to
               evaluate the effect of a strong CYP3A inducer on ensartinib exposure to inform appropriate dose
               recommendation when they are concomitantly used.

               Gastric Acid Reducing Agents
               Based on the pH-solubility data for ensartinib listed in Table 42 and the pH-solubility curve
               shown in Figure 7, ensartinib is completely soluble from pH 1.2 to 4.5 given the solubility values
               are greater than 0.9 mg/mL (225 mg ensartinib in 250 mL gastric fluid).

               Food Effect
               FDA agrees with the Applicant’s proposal of administering ensartinib without regard to food
               intake as a high fat and high calorie meal (total 800-1000 calories, >50% fat) had no clinical
               meaningful effect on ensartinib PK based on the results from the food-effect Study BTP-44313.
               Briefly, mean Cmax and AUC0-inf were lower after a meal compared to those in the fasting
               condition following a single ensartinib dose of 225 mg (Refer to Table 7 in Section 5.2.2).
               Considering the magnitude of the change in ensartinib exposure and the range of 90% CI, the
               overall changes in AUC0-inf and Cmax in the fed condition are not expected to be clinically
               meaningful.
               The median value (minimum, maximum) of Tmax after a high-fat meal (6 hr (4.5 hr, 12 hr)) is
               longer than the mean Tmax (4.5 hr (4 hr, 8 hr)) under fasting condition.


                    8.3. Plans for Pediatric Drug Development
               Under the Pediatric Research Equity Act (PREA) (21 U.S.C. 355c) and the amendment to PREA,
               FDA Reauthorization Act of 2017 (Amendments to Sec. 505B of the Federal Food, Drug, and
               Cosmetic Act) all applications for new active ingredients, new indications, new dosage forms,
               new dosing regimens, or new routes of administration are required to contain an assessment of
               the safety and effectiveness of the product for the claimed indication(s) and evaluation of
               molecular targeted oncology drugs in pediatric patients unless this requirement is waived,
               deferred, or inapplicable. As agreed upon in the initial pediatric study plan, FDA concluded that
               a molecularly targeted investigation in pediatric patients was required under the revised
               provisions of FDA Reauthorization Act of 2017 under PREA.
               The Applicant proposed to fulfill the requirement of a molecularly targeted investigation through
               submission of the reports from the Pediatric MATCH subprotocol F, an activity-estimating study
               of ensartinib in pediatric and young adult patients with advanced or metastatic solid tumors,
               primary CNS tumors, non-Hodgkin lymphomas and histiocytoses, with ALK, or ROS1
               alterations. This study is currently ongoing.
               The Applicant has requested a deferral of submission of the required pediatric study because the
               product is ready for approval for use in adults and the pediatric study has not been completed. A
               PMR for the submission of the report of the molecularly targeted investigation in pediatric
               patients will be included in the approval letter. A partial waiver will be granted for children <5
               years of age, given the feasibility of enrolling younger patients with relapsed or refractory
               disease due to disease rarity and the existence of multiple competing trials.

               maternal toxicity (reduced body weight and food consumption), increased pre- and post-
               implantation loss, decreased fetal body weight (-9.5% compared to control, p≤0.05) and numbers
               of live fetuses, and fetal visceral variations including missing renal papillae and pyelectasis.
               The pharmacology/ toxicology team therefore recommends a warning in the ensartinib label for
               embryo-fetal toxicity. Consistent with the recommendations for teratogenic or embryo-lethal but
               non-genotoxic drugs described in the FDA Guidance for Industry, Oncology Pharmaceuticals:
               Reproductive Toxicity Testing and Labeling Recommendations (May 2019), and considering the
               mean ensartinib half-life of 30 hours, FDA recommends advising males and females of
               reproductive potential use effective contraception during treatment with ENSACOVE and for
               one week after the last dose.

               Lactation
               There are no data regarding ensartinib or its metabolites in breastmilk. Because of the potential
               for serious adverse reactions in breastfed children, the nonclinical review team recommends
               advising patients not to breastfeed during treatment with ensartinib and for 1 week after the last
               dose.

                             13.1.4.1. General Toxicology
               To assess the safety of ensartinib, the Applicant conducted repeat-dose toxicology studies up to
               13 weeks in duration in rats and dogs.

               Repeat-Dose Toxicity
               13-Week Oral Gavage Toxicity and Toxicokinetic Study with X-396 in Rats with a 4 Week
               Recovery (Study # X396-TOX-006).

               Key Study Findings
                    •   There was no drug-related mortality.
                    •   The major target organ was skin. Ensartinib induced hair thinning/loss and scabbing,
                        which correlated microscopically with minimal hyperkeratosis and slight mixed cell
                        inflammation in the skin and showed evidence of recovery.
                    •   Ensartinib decreased mean white blood cells, lymphocytes, eosinophils, basophils, and
                        leukocytes, which persisted in females during the recovery period.
                    •   Ensartinib increased liver enzymes at ≥12.5 mg/kg in males and females and was not
                        fully reversible in females. Increased enzymes did not correlate with histologic findings
                        in the liver.

               Findings from the good laboratory practice (GLP)-compliant 4-week repeat-dose toxicology
               studies in rats (Study # X396-TOX-004) and dogs (Study # X396-TOX-005) were generally
               consistent with the 13-week toxicology studies. Higher doses of ensartinib were evaluated in the
               4-week studies, resulting in mortality in rats at 150 mg/kg/day due to overall poor health (weight
               loss, severe skin lesions, inflammation). Additional findings in the 4-week rat study included
               increased creatine kinase levels and histologic chronic/active inflammation in the heart,
               inflammation in the lungs, and hyperkeratosis in the stomach. Mortality was seen in the 4-week
               dog study at 60 mg/kg/day. Additional findings in the 4-week dog study included increased
               creatine kinase, histologic lymphoid depletion in the spleen, and up to marked hypocellularity of
               the bone marrow.
