                  15.4. COMPOSER (Study BP39144)
               Study Design
               COMPOSER is a first-in-human study that consists of four sequential parts and an OLE designed
               to evaluate the safety, tolerability, PK, and PD of crovalimab in healthy male volunteers (Part 1)
               and in patients with PNH (Parts 2, 3, 4 and the OLE). Part 1 was a randomized, adaptive,
               placebo-controlled, parallel group study in HVs who received single IV or SC doses of
               crovalimab or placebo. This part was observer-blinded (the investigators and all individuals in
               direct contact with subjects at the investigative site will be blinded, except the pharmacist
               handling the study drug). Part 2 was an open-label, multiple-dose, multicenter, intraindividual
               dose escalation study in patients with PNH who were treatment-naïve. Part 3 was an open-label,
               multiple-dose, multicenter study in patients with PNH who switched from eculizumab. Part 4 is
               an open-label, multicenter, two-arm (Arm A: treatment-naïve, Arm B: patients previously treated
               with eculizumab) nonrandomized study in patients with PNH.

               Open-Label Extension
               Subjects who complete 20 weeks of treatment and derive benefit have the option to enter the
               OLE period. Subjects transitioning from Parts 2, 3, or 4 are to initially remain on the same SC
               dose regimen as they were previously receiving and transition to crovalimab dosing that is
               consistent with the proposed crovalimab dose regimen. IV rescue doses of crovalimab are
               allowed, consistent with COMMODORE-1 and COMMODORE-2.
               The primary objective is to evaluate safety, tolerability, and PD effects of crovalimab on
               complement activity in patients with PNH. Secondary objectives include characterization of
               pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics, evaluation of immunogenicity and assessment of efficacy
               as measured by change in LDH, free-hemoglobin and stabilized hemoglobin levels.

               Efficacy Results
               The co-primary efficacy endpoints of hemolysis control and TA were met at the time of the
               CCOD. The mean proportion of subjects with hemolysis control (i.e., LDH ≤1.5×ULN) from
               Week 5 through Week 25 was 78.7% (95% CI: 67.8%, 86.6%), which met the prespecified
               success criterion of 60% (based on the point estimate of the 95% CI of the treatment effect of
               eculizumab) and a success criterion of 66.9% (based on the lower bound of the 95% CI of the
               treatment effect of eculizumab) for the lower limit of the two-sided 95% CI. The difference in
               the proportion of subjects with TA from baseline through Week 25 and within 24 weeks prior to
               screening was 51.0% (95% CI: 34.3%, 65.1%), which was statistically significant (p<0.0001) at
               the prespecified, 2-sided type I error level of 0.05.

               Pharmacodynamic/Biomarker Results
               Due to COVID-19 travel restrictions, approximately half of subjects were missing the required
               PD and biomarker assessments for each visit after Week 25. For the subjects that had PD and
               biomarker assessments, complement levels, as measured by free C5 concentrations, were
               reduced from a mean baseline level of 226.6 mg/L to mean levels of <0.1 mg/L from Week 2 of
               crovalimab treatment, providing evidence of complete inhibition of free C5. The low levels of
               free C5 were sustained up to Week 49. Terminal complement activity (CH50) was reduced from
               a mean baseline level of 48 U/mL (SD: 11.7 U/mL) to levels near or BLQ (i.e., <10 U/mL) from
               Week 2 of treatment with crovalimab, providing evidence of complete inhibition of terminal
               complement activity.
               Clone size was also evaluated, and the RBC PNH clone size (Type II
               glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-dim and TYPE III GPI-negative erythrocytes) increased from
               mean baseline levels of 46.9% (SD: 22.2%) to 69.6% (SD: 24.1%) at Week 25, consistent with
               decreased hemolysis of GPI-deficient PNH cells.

                  16.4. COMPOSER (Study BP39144)
               Study Results
               The COMPOSER study is being conducted in Japan, Germany, Hungary, Korea, France, Italy,
               and the Netherlands. The first subject was enrolled on November 14, 2016. The CCOD was
               November 1, 2021. A total of 59 subjects (HVs: 15 subjects, subjects with PNH: 44 subjects
               [treatment-naïve: 18 subjects, subjects who switched from eculizumab: 26 subjects]) were
               enrolled in the study.
               In Part 1, a total of 15 subjects were enrolled in three cohorts. In each cohort, 5 healthy adult
               male volunteers were randomized (3:2) to receive a single IV (Cohorts 1 [75 mg] and 2
               [125 mg]) or SC (Cohort 3 [100 mg]) dose of crovalimab or placebo. Most of the subjects were
               White (80.0%) and the age by cohort ranged from 29 to 43 years (range: 21 to 52).
               In Part 2, a total of 10 adult subjects with PNH who were treatment-naïve were enrolled.
               Subjects received 3, single, ascending IV doses of crovalimab: 375 mg on Day 1, 500 mg on Day
               8, and 1000 mg on Day 22. The first SC dose of crovalimab 170 mg administration was initiated
               on Day 36, followed by weekly 170 mg SC injections for a total of 20 weeks. The majority of
               subjects enrolled in Part 2 were male (60.0%) and White (70.0%). The median age was 52.5
               years (range: 35 to 74 years) and median weight was 66.9 kg (range: 58.9 to 98.0 kg). There
               were 3 out of 10 subjects with a history of RBC transfusion up to 1 year prior to starting study
               treatment, with a median of 2 units of transfused RBC (range: 2 to 6). The median treatment
               duration was 1520 days (range: 1226 to 1618).
               In Part 3, a total of 19 adult subjects with PNH who were previously treated with eculizumab
               were randomly assigned to three different treatment schedules (Arm A: 7 subjects, Arm B: 6
               subjects, Arm C: 6 subjects) with an ongoing assessment of safety, tolerability, PK, and PD data.
               All subjects received a loading dose of 1000 mg crovalimab IV 2 weeks after the last dose of
               eculizumab. Starting on Day 8, two subjects in Arm A initially received crovalimab 680 mg SC
               Q4W. After observing possible DTDC-related AEs, the dosing regimen was modified to 170 mg
               SC weekly for the first 8 doses. At dose 9 (Day 64), subjects started maintenance regimen of
               680 mg SC Q4W. Subjects in Arm B received crovalimab 340 mg SC biweekly, and subjects in
               Arm C received crovalimab 170 mg SC every week. Most of the subjects enrolled in Part 3 were
               male (68.4%) and White (47.4%) or Asian (36.8%). The median age was 46 years (range: 33 to
               69 years). The median weight was 78.2 kg (range: 40.6 to 131.5 kg). Eight of 19 subjects had a
               history of RBC transfusion up to 1 year prior to randomization, with a median of 5 units of
               transfused RBC (range: 1 to 21). The median treatment duration was 1197 days (range: 134 to
               1435).
               In Part 4, a total of 15 adult subjects (Arm A: 8 treatment-naïve, Arm B: 7 subjects previously
               treated with eculizumab) were enrolled. Subjects received a loading series comprised of 1000 mg
               crovalimab IV on Day 1, followed by 340 mg SC on Days 2, 8, 15, and 22. From Day 29
               onwards, all subjects received 680 mg SC Q4W. The median treatment duration of crovalimab in
               Part 4 was 2.23 years (range: 0.92 to 2.46). In the treatment-naïve Arm A, most subjects were
               male (75.0%) and Asian (50.0%) or White (37.5%). The median age was 55.5 years (range: 42 to
               73). The median weight was 80.1 kg (range: 56.7 to 100 kg). There were 4 out of 8 subjects with
               a history of RBC transfusion up to 1 year prior to starting study treatment, with a median of 7
               units of transfused RBC (range: 2 to 198). The median treatment duration of Arm A was 827

               Open-Label Extension Period
               Among the 44 subjects with PNH, a total of 43 subjects (treatment-naïve: 18 subjects, subjects
               who switched from eculizumab: 25 subjects) entered the OLE period. Subjects enrolling in the
               OLE from Parts 2, 3, and 4 initially stayed on the previously assigned treatment schedule. With
               the implementation of the tiered-weight dosing, introduced during a protocol amendment, all
               subjects in the OLE who were not currently receiving Q4W dosing were required to switch to the
               Q4W dosing regimen. Subjects either received 680 mg SC Q4W (BW ≥40 kg to <100 kg) or
               1020 mg SC Q4W (BW ≥100 kg).
               As of the CCOD (November 1, 2021), a total of 38 subjects were reported to be receiving
               treatment with crovalimab in the OLE (17 subjects who are treatment-naïve and 21 subjects who
               switched from eculizumab). The median treatment duration of crovalimab in the 44 subjects with
               PNH to the CCOD was 3.03 years (range: 0.4 to 4.4).

               Efficacy Results
               For the OLE period of COMPOSER, only exploratory efficacy endpoints of hemolysis control
               (change in LDH), TA, stabilized hemoglobin, and BTH were analyzed. Because no formal
               efficacy evaluation was prespecified for the study, results were descriptive in nature and should
               be interpreted with caution. During the OLE period, key efficacy results (i.e., evaluated from
               Week 20 to the CCOD) were as follows:
               •    Mean normalized LDH was generally maintained below 1.5×ULN and 80% to 100% of
                    subjects at each visit had LDH ≤1.5×ULN.
               •    Across the 24-week intervals, the proportion of subjects achieving TA (82.9% to 91.7%) and
                    hemoglobin stabilization (79.5% to 87.5%) remained stable.
               Across the 24-week intervals, 0.0% to 4.9% of subjects reported a BTH event.

               consciousness. A CT scan established the diagnosis of subdural hematoma with cerebral hernia.
               Emergency treatment was administered; however, potentially life-saving brain surgery was
               denied by the family. In the afternoon of the same day, the subject died with a diagnosis of Grade
               5 subdural hematoma.
               For deaths that occurred in COMMODORE-1 and COMMODORE-2, see Section 7.6.1.2.

                        17.1.1.6. Subgroup Analyses, Pooled Analyses, COMMODORE-1,
                               COMMODORE-2, and COMMODORE-3
               Subgroup safety analyses by age, race, region, and sex were conducted using the pooled data of
               COMMODORE-1, COMMODORE-2, and COMMODORE-3 to evaluate if the results were
               consistent across the subgroups. The results should be interpreted with caution due to small
               sample sizes.

               Age
               In the crovalimab Phase 3 studies, a total of 11 subjects (2.9%) were <18 years of age, 327
               subjects (86.7%) were 18 to 64 years of age, and 39 subjects (10.3%) were ≥65 years of age. The
               safety results of crovalimab-naïve and switch groups by age are summarized in Table 137. The
               safety profile of crovalimab-naïve and switch groups was broadly similar between the 18-to-64-
               year and ≥65-year age groups. In the crovalimab-naïve group, however, the incidence of TEAEs
               was higher in the 18-to-64-year age group compared with the ≥65-year age group (91.8% versus
               76.9%). In the crovalimab switch group, subjects who were ≥65 years of age had higher
               incidences of serious TEAEs (30.8%) and Grade 3/4 TEAEs (46.2%) compared with subjects
               who were 18 to 64 years of age (serious TEAEs: 13.4%, Grade 3/4 TEAEs: 21.7%).

               Pediatric Subjects
               At the primary CCOD of November 16, 2022, a total of 11 pediatric subjects (crovalimab-naïve:
               9 subjects, crovalimab-switch: 2 subjects) received crovalimab across the crovalimab Phase 3
               trials (COMMODORE-1 [crovalimab-switch: 1 subject in the nonrandomized arm],
               COMMODORE-2 [crovalimab-naïve: 6 subjects in the nonrandomized arm, crovalimab-switch:
               1 subject during the extension period], COMMODORE-3 [crovalimab-naïve: 3 subjects]). In the
               11 pediatric subjects, the baseline age ranged from 13 to 17 years and weight ranged from 49 to
               99 kg. A total of six subjects were females, nine subjects were Asian, one subject was White, and
               one had an unknown race. Treatment-emergent AEs were reported in a total of 9 pediatric
               subjects (81.8%). Most TEAEs were Grade 1 or 2 in severity. Grade 3 TEAEs occurred in a total
               of two pediatric crovalimab-naïve subjects in COMMODORE-3 (one subject had a Grade 3
               blood bilirubin increase and another subject had a Grade 3 neutrophil count decrease). All Grade
               3 events resolved without dose modification of the study treatment. No pediatric subjects
               experienced Grade 4 or 5 TEAEs or TEAEs that were considered serious.
               No cases of meningococcal infections were reported across all crovalimab PNH studies.
               However, there was one case of meningococcal meningitis reported in Study BO42354, a study
               evaluating the efficacy, safety, PK, and PD of crovalimab in pediatric patients with atypical
               hemolytic uremic syndrome. The pediatric subject experienced meningococcal meningitis on
               Day 430 (Grade 3). The pathogen was identified as Neisseria meningitidis serotype X (the
               subject was vaccinated against serotype ACWY). The event subsequently resolved after 4 days,
               with no change to crovalimab treatment.

               Race and Region
               Most of the subjects in the Phase 3 crovalimab studies were Asian (59.9%) or White (35.5%) and
               were enrolled from Asia (59.2%) or Europe (31.6%). The safety results of crovalimab (naïve and
               switch) were generally similar between subjects who were Asian and White and between
               subjects enrolled from Asia and Europe. In the crovalimab-naïve group, the incidence of Grade 3
               or 4 TEAEs was higher in Asians (28.9%) compared with Whites (17.8%). The differences were
               mostly due to higher incidences of Grade 3 or 4 TEAEs in Asians in the blood and lymphatic
               system disorders system organ class (SOC) (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia) and
               liver injury.

                  17.2. COMPOSER (Study BP39144)
               COMPOSER is an adaptive Phase 1/2 study to evaluate the safety, efficacy, PK, and PD of
               crovalimab in HVs and patients with PNH. The trial design is presented in Section 16.2.

               Part 4
               The evaluation of safety was conducted for Part 4 of the study since Part 4 administered
               crovalimab at the proposed dose regimen. The crovalimab proposed dose regimen was
               administered in 15 adult subjects with PNH (Arm A: 8 treatment-naïve, Arm B: 7 subjects
               previously treated with eculizumab). The median treatment duration of crovalimab in Part 4 was
               2.23 years (range: 0.92 to 2.46). Table 141 summarizes the overall safety results of Part 4.
               Severity of TEAEs was classified as mild, moderate, or severe.
               No deaths or TEAEs leading to discontinuation or treatment modification of the study drug
               occurred in the study. Serious TEAEs occurred in a total of 3 subjects (20.0%) (crovalimab-
               naïve: 2 subjects [myocardial infarction and BTH], crovalimab-switch: 1 subject [erysipelas]).
               TEAEs occurred in 93.3% of subjects and most of the TEAEs were mild (20.0%) or moderate
               (66.7%) in severity. One subject in the crovalimab-naïve group had severe BTH. Overall, the
               most frequently reported TEAs (≥20%) were headache, arthralgia, asthenia/fatigue, backpain,
               gastroenteritis, nasopharyngitis and peripheral edema, consistent with those reported in
               COMMODORE-2 and COMMODORE-1.
               One subject in the crovalimab-naïve group experienced type III hypersensitivity reaction (mild
               rash erythematous) at time of switch from crovalimab to eculizumab, after discontinuing from
               the study due to a lack of efficacy. The event of type III hypersensitivity reaction resolved.
               No cases of meningococcal meningitis or hypersensitivity (other than type III hypersensitivity
               reactions) were reported in subjects with PNH during the study.
               Overall, the safety profile of crovalimab was generally consistent with the results of the Phase 3
               studies.

                  17.3. Additional Safety Explorations
               Electrocardiograms and QT
               No QTc prolongation was observed in the concentration-QTc analysis. Based on the
               concentration-QT analysis from COMPOSER and the Phase 3 studies, COMMODORE-1,
               COMMODORE-2, and COMMODORE-3 in treatment-naïve and switch subjects with PNH, a
               statistically significant decrease (p=0.0097) in ΔQTcF was found with increasing crovalimab
               concentrations. However, the effect was very small (ΔQTcF of 5.42 ms at a crovalimab
               concentration of 600 mcg/mL) in relation to the overall variability, and not in the direction of
               clinical concern (i.e., lower ΔQTcF at higher exposure). For details, refer to the Cardiac Safety
               Studies Review, dated April 9, 2024.

               Human Carcinogenicity and Tumor Development
               In the Phase 3 PNH crovalimab clinical studies, a total of 10 subjects (2.7%, crovalimab-naïve: 7
               subjects, crovalimab-switch: 3 subjects) developed TEAEs in the “neoplasms benign, malignant
               and unspecified (incl cysts and polyps)” Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities SOC while
               receiving crovalimab. The TEAEs were colorectal cancer, desmoid tumor, lipoma, lung
               neoplasm, mantle cell lymphoma, melanocytic naevus, neoplasm, prostate cancer, skin neoplasm
               bleeding, and thyroid cancer, in one subject each. Time to onset ranged from 86 to 367 days from
               the start of crovalimab treatment. The outcome was fatal for the subject who had colorectal
               cancer (see Section 7.6.1.3) The TEAEs did not recover/resolve in 3 subjects and did
               recover/resolve in 6 subjects. Carcinogenesis and mutagenesis studies have not been performed
               with crovalimab to establish the genotoxic potential of crovalimab. However, as noted in
               Section 7.1, the risk of carcinogenicity for crovalimab is considered low based on a weight-of-
               evidence risk assessment.

               Pediatrics and Assessment of Effects on Growth
               A total of 12 pediatric subjects (crovalimab-naïve: 9 subjects, crovalimab-switch: 3 subjects)
               with PNH (13 to 17 years of age and BW ≥40 kg) received crovalimab in the Phase 3 clinical
               trials. There was no evidence to suggest that the safety and efficacy of crovalimab would be
               different between pediatric and adult patients with PNH weighing ≥40 kg. See Sections 6.3.4 and

               Overdose, Drug Abuse Potential, Withdrawal, and Rebound
               No events of overdose were reported in subjects who received crovalimab in the PNH clinical
               studies. No dedicated studies on the potential for crovalimab to cause dependence were
               performed. Based on the pharmacological properties and the TEAE profile of crovalimab, there
               is no evidence to suggest that there are risks of abuse with crovalimab.
               Similar to other C5 inhibitors (eculizumab and ravulizumab), monitoring PNH manifestations
               after discontinuation of crovalimab will be listed as a Warning and Precaution in the label. It is
               recommended to monitor patients after discontinuation of the C5 treatment to detect hemolysis.
               Patients with PNH who discontinue crovalimab should be closely monitored for signs and
               symptoms of serious IVH, identified by elevated LDH levels, along with a sudden decrease in
               hemoglobin or re-appearance of symptoms such as fatigue, hemoglobinuria, abdominal pain,
               dyspnea, MAVEs (including thrombosis), dysphagia, or erectile dysfunction. If signs and
               symptoms of hemolysis occur after discontinuation of crovalimab, restarting treatment with
               crovalimab should be considered, if appropriate, or initiating another treatment for PNH.
               Patients who discontinue crovalimab and soon thereafter, start treatment with other C5 inhibitors
               (i.e., eculizumab or ravulizumab) that bind different epitopes of C5, are at risk of DTDC-
               associated type III hypersensitivity reactions. See Section 7.6.1.8.4.

               Deaths
               In the 120-day safety update, a total of four additional deaths were reported in the total
               crovalimab population. Of the four deaths, three deaths occurred in the crovalimab-naïve
               population in COMMODORE-2 due to COVID-19, COVID-19 pneumonia, and death due to
               unknown cause (subject died in his sleep and had no symptoms in the days preceding death, with
               normal hematologic laboratory data; an autopsy was not performed) and one death in a subject in
               COMMODORE-2 who was treated with eculizumab during the primary treatment period,
               switched to crovalimab, and died during the extension period due to pneumonia aspiration. After
               the CCOD of the 120-day safety update (May 31, 2023), one additional death was reported in the
               crovalimab-switch population in COMMODORE-2. The subject had a subdural hematoma that
               had a fatal outcome on June 9, 2023. This subject was a 33-year-old Asian female with a history
               of MDS. At baseline, the subject had Grade 2 thrombocytopenia and Grade 1 neutropenia. It was
               reported that MDS worsened on Day 99 (with thrombocytopenia worsening to Grade 3) and on
               Day 210 (with thrombocytopenia worsening to Grade 4 and neutropenia to Grade 2). The event
               of worsening MDS and thrombocytopenia was not resolved at the time of death. It was also
               reported that this subject had a urinary tract infection 3 months before death, which may have
               further contributed to ongoing platelet consumption and bleeding events (e.g., epistaxis and
               heavy menstrual bleeding) before the fatal event. On Day 648, the subject was admitted to the
               emergency department and a review of the brain CT scan showed several acute subdural
               hematomas. On Day 657, the subject died after experiencing progression of acute subdural
               hematomas, with a brain CT scan showing multiple, new intraparenchymal lobar hemorrhages. It
               is likely that the subdural hematoma, and subsequent subarachnoid and cerebral bleeding, were
               caused by thrombocytopenia due to underlying MDS (i.e., deteriorating marrow function).

               Subgroup Analyses

               Age
               Based on the 120-day safety update, of the 393 subjects treated with crovalimab in
               COMMODORE-1, 2, and 3, a total of 12 subjects (3.1%) were younger than 18 years of age, 338
               subjects (86%) were 18 to 64 years of age, and 43 subjects (10.9%) were 65 years of age and
               older. The incidences of fatal SAEs were higher in subjects ≥65 years of age (9.3%) compared to
               subjects aged 18 to 64 years (1.2%). The incidences of serious adverse reactions were also higher
               in subjects who were 65 years and older (crovalimab-naïve: 7.7%, crovalimab-switch: 6.7%)
               compared to subjects who were 18 to 64 years of age (crovalimab-naïve: 3.5%, crovalimab-
               switch: 3.6%). The safety profile of crovalimab by age was consistent with the results reported in
               the initial BLA. It is unclear whether the higher incidence of SAEs in the >65 age group is due to
               the study drug or simply reflects background AEs in an older population.

               Race
               In the total crovalimab population, the majority of subjects were Asian (58%) and White
               (36.9%). The incidences of TEAEs were similar between different races (Asian: 93.0%,
               White: 93.1%, Black/African American: 100%). The safety profile of crovalimab was generally
               similar across different races, and consistent with those reported in the initial BLA.

               Sex
               In the total crovalimab population, approximately half (48.3%) were female. The proportion of
               subjects who experienced at least one TEAE (male: 91.1%, female: 95.3%) was comparable
               between males and females and consistent with those reported in the initial BLA.

                   17.6. Additional Analyses for Type III
                       Hypersensitivity Reactions
               Fifteen subjects had a time interval between the last dose of the C5 inhibitor and the first dose of
               crovalimab being outside of the expected dosing intervals of eculizumab (14±2 days) or
               ravulizumab (56±2 days), and three of them experienced a type III hypersensitivity reaction.
               •    Specifically, all three subjects with a type III hypersensitivity reaction switched from
                    ravulizumab and had a time interval of 49, 51, and 114 days between the last dose of
                    ravulizumab and the first dose of crovalimab.
               •    Severity of these type III hypersensitivity reaction events ranged between Grade 1 to 3
                    (Grade 1 event occurred in a subject with time interval of 49 days, Grade 2 event in a subject
                    with time interval of 51 days and Grade 3 event in a subject with time interval of 114 days).
                    Signs and symptoms of type III hypersensitivity reactions in these subjects were consistent
                    with what was observed in the total switch population and all events were resolved as of the
                    CCOD of May 31, 2023.
               The number of subjects with a time interval between the last dose of the C5 inhibitor and the first
               dose of crovalimab being outside of the expected dosing intervals of eculizumab or ravulizumab
               and experiencing a type III hypersensitivity reaction is limited. Therefore, it is not possible to
               reach a conclusion on whether this influences occurrence, severity, or reversibility of type III
               hypersensitivity reactions. With limited data, no correlation was observed between the time from
               the last dose of prior C5 inhibitor treatment and the first crovalimab dose, and the onset, severity,
               or reversibility of type III hypersensitivity reactions.

                  I. Executive Summary

               1. Summary of Regulatory Action
               New drug application (NDA) 218275 for ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection was
               submitted by Basilea Pharmaceutica International Ltd, Allschwil (Applicant) for the following
               indications:
               1. Treatment of adult patients with Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (SAB), including those
                  with right-sided infective endocarditis (RIE)
               2. Treatment of adult patients with acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI)
               3. Treatment of adult and pediatric patients (greater than or equal to 3 months to less than
                  18 years of age) with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP)
               The application was reviewed by the multidisciplinary review team. The review team has
               recommended approval, and I, the signatory for this application, concur with this
               recommendation.
               Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is a cephalosporin antibacterial drug which exerts its antibacterial
               activity by binding to penicillin-binding proteins and inhibiting synthesis of the bacterial cell
               wall. Ceftobiprole medocaril is the prodrug that rapidly converts to its active moiety,
               ceftobiprole. Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is the salt form of ceftobiprole medocaril;
               ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is used interchangeably with ceftobiprole throughout this review.
               Ceftobiprole demonstrated in vitro and clinical activity against gram-positive and gram-negative
               bacteria including methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) and methicillin-resistant S. aureus
               (MRSA), Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae,
               Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Klebsiella pneumonia and Escherichia coli.
               The Applicant submitted a single, phase 3, randomized, double-blinded, active-controlled,
               noninferiority trial in adults for each of the indications (SAB, ABSSSI, and CABP) that
               demonstrated noninferiority to the comparators. Additionally, the Applicant submitted a phase 3,
               randomized, active-controlled trial in pediatric subjects with CABP and hospital-acquired
               bacterial pneumonia (HABP) and a phase 3 trial in adults with HABP and ventilator-associated
               bacterial pneumonia (VABP). Data from the pediatric CABP/HABP trial were primarily used to
               support the safety of ceftobiprole in pediatric subjects with CABP with efficacy extrapolated
               from the adult CABP trial. Indications for HABP/VABP in adults and HABP in pediatric
               subjects were not sought in this application and the data from the HABP/VABP subjects
               informed safety assessments.
               The safety database consisted of 464 subjects who received at least one dose of ceftobiprole in
               phase 1 studies, and 1315 total subjects who received at least one dose of ceftobiprole at the to-
               be-marketed dose in the phase 3 trials. Overall, the safety findings observed with ceftobiprole
               were similar to other FDA-approved cephalosporins. The risks can be mitigated through labeling
               and further evaluated during routine pharmacovigilance.

               1. Adult patients with SAB, including those with right-sided infective endocarditis (RIE),

               2. Adult patients with ABSSSI caused by susceptible isolates of the following gram-positive
                  and gram-negative microorganisms: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible and
                  methicillin-resistant isolates), Streptococcus pyogenes, and Klebsiella pneumoniae
               3. Adult and pediatric patients (3 months to less than 18 years old) with CABP caused by
                  susceptible isolates of the following gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms:
                  Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus
                  influenzae, Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Escherichia coli, and Klebsiella pneumoniae
               The drug product established name and strength will be expressed in terms of the salt (i.e.,
               ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection, 667 mg/vial) and labeling will include a statement
               stating that 667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 500 mg of ceftobiprole (the
               active metabolite). This is an exception to the USP Salt Policy to eliminate having three
               different names/strengths in labeling (i.e., based on the prodrug, salt form, and active
               metabolite), thereby reducing the possibility for medication errors and harmonizing the US FDA
               labeling with existing medical literature and product labeling from other countries.
               For detailed information supporting the basis for this approval, please refer to the reviews
               included in this interdisciplinary assessment and the product quality review.

                    2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
               All three of the proposed indications (SAB, ABSSSI, and CABP) are serious and often life-
               threatening infections with significant morbidity and mortality. While there are multiple
               antibacterial drugs currently approved to treat ABSSSI and CABP, the continued evolution of
               antibacterial resistance mechanisms, drug-drug interactions, and adverse effects of available
               antibacterial drugs can limit treatment options. There is an urgent need to develop antibacterial
               drugs which cover both gram-negative and gram-positive organisms, especially MRSA, which is
               a major cause of hospital and community-acquired infections worldwide . Current treatments for
               MRSA infections have certain limitations (e.g., vancomycin is associated with nephrotoxicity
               and the need for drug monitoring, linezolid has certain drug-drug interactions and toxicities,
               daptomycin does not penetrate the lung parenchyma, and ceftaroline is not FDA-approved for
               difficult to treat infections such as bacteremia and RIE). Approved treatments for SAB, including
               RIE due to MRSA are especially limited.
               Ceftobiprole, an advanced generation cephalosporin antibacterial drug would provide an
               effective treatment option with a favorable safety profile for the indications sought (SAB,
               ABSSSI, and CABP). The Applicant submitted data demonstrating safety and effectiveness for
               all three indications.
               Trial BPR-CS-009 demonstrated that ceftobiprole is noninferior to daptomycin ± aztreonam in
               the treatment of subjects with SAB, including those with RIE, caused by methicillin-susceptible
               and methicillin-resistant isolates in regard to the primary endpoint of overall success based on
               data review committee assessment at the post-treatment evaluation visit in the modified intent-to-
               treat population (ceftobiprole 69.8%, daptomycin 68.7% [difference 2.0%; 95% confidence
               interval (CI): -7.1, 11.1]), which met the prespecified 15% noninferiority (NI) margin.
               Trial BPR-CS-008 demonstrated that ceftobiprole is noninferior to vancomycin plus aztreonam
               in the treatment of subjects with ABSSSI with respect to the primary endpoint of early clinical
               response in the intent-to-treat population (ceftobiprole 91.3%, vancomycin plus aztreonam
               88.1% [difference 3.3%; 95% CI: -1.2, 7.8]), which met the prespecified 10% NI margin.
               Trial CAP-3001 demonstrated that ceftobiprole is noninferior to ceftriaxone ± linezolid in the
               treatment of adult subjects with CABP. In the intent-to-treat population, the clinical cure rate in
               the ceftobiprole group was 76.4% compared with the comparator group at 79.3% with a
               treatment difference of -2.9%, 95 CI (-9.3, 3.6), which met the prespecified 10% NI margin.
               Efficacy for CABP in the pediatric population was extrapolated from the adult CABP Trial.
               The safety database for ceftobiprole was adequate for the proposed dosing regimens, intended
               subject populations, and respective indications. Generally, the Applicant provided data
               demonstrating that the safety of ceftobiprole was similar to the active comparator in each trial.
               Overall, ceftobiprole has a favorable safety profile, and safety findings can be adequately
               addressed in labeling and by routine pharmacovigilance.

                  II. Interdisciplinary Assessment

               3. Introduction
               Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection (Zevtera) is a cephalosporin antibacterial drug that
               binds to penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits their transpeptidase activity. The active
               ingredient (drug substance), ceftobiprole medocaril sodium, is a salt of a prodrug, ceftobiprole
               medocaril, and the active metabolite is ceftobiprole. The dosage form of the drug product is a
               powder for injection. Ceftobiprole is currently approved in several countries outside of the US
               for the treatment of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP) and hospital-acquired
               bacterial pneumonia (HABP).
               Ceftobiprole was submitted under new drug application (NDA) 022132 for treatment of
               complicated skin and skin structure infections by the previous Applicant, Johnson and Johnson
               Pharmaceutical Research & Development LLC (J&J) on May 18, 2007. NDA 022132 received
               an Approvable Letter on March 17, 2008, a Complete Response Letter on November 21, 2008,
               and a Complete Response Letter on December 28, 2009. The Clinical Deficiencies cited in these
               letters concerned studies BAP 00154 and BAP 00414 which are not included in this new NDA
               218275. Ownership of NDA 022132 was transferred back to Basilea Pharmaceutica Ltd. on
               January 24, 2011.
               Ceftobiprole medocaril for injection was granted Qualified Infectious Disease Product
               designation for the CABP, acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI), and
               Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (SAB) indications on July 20, 2015, August 7, 2015, and
               December 8, 2017, respectively. Refer to Section 12 for a more detailed regulatory summary.
               In this NDA submission, the proposed indications are for the treatment of adult patients with
               SAB, including right-sided infective endocarditis (RIE), ABSSSI, and CABP and for treatment
               of pediatric patients 3 months to less than 18 years old with CABP. For current available
               therapies and typical pathogens for each indication, refer to Section 2.1.
               All three indications were supported by phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, active
               controlled noninferiority (NI) trials which met their respective primary endpoints within the
               prespecified NI margins. Refer to Section 6 and 7 for reviews of efficacy and safety for each
               trial.

               The proposed dosing regimen is ceftobiprole 500 mg every 6 hours on Days 1 to 8, followed by
               every 8 hours from Day 9 up to 42 days for SAB and 500 mg every 8 hours for 5 to 14 days for
               ABSSSI and CABP with dosing adjustments based on renal function. The initial proposal by the
               Applicant was based on the strength of the amount of the “active moiety/metabolite” as 500 mg
               ceftobiprole/vial.
               During the NDA review, the OPQ team recommended that the drug product established name
               and strength be revised following the USP Salt Policy to express the amount of the prodrug
               neutral form (i.e., ceftobiprole medocaril for injection, 646 mg/vial). In response, the Applicant
               requested exemption from the USP Salt Policy following the example of a previously approved
               product which was also a salt of a prodrug, Cresemba (isavuconazonium sulfate), for which the
               strength is expressed in terms of the salt in approved labeling.
               The clinical team and the Division of Medication and Error Prevention Analysis (DMEPA)
               agreed with the Applicant that an exception to the USP Salt Policy would eliminate having three
               different names/strengths in labeling (i.e., based on the prodrug, salt form, and active
               metabolite), thereby reducing the possibility for medication errors and also harmonizing the US
               FDA labeling with existing medical literature and product labeling from other countries. Upon
               further discussion of the drug product name and strength between the Office of New Drugs
               (OND) and Office of Policy and Pharmaceutical Quality (OPPQ) teams, a consensus was
               reached that the drug product established name and strength should be expressed in terms of the
               salt (i.e., ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection, 667 mg/vial) and labeling would include a
               statement stating that 667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 500 mg of
               ceftobiprole. For details regarding this decision, refer to the Memorandum filed in DARRTS on
               3/21/24 by Jibril Abdus-Samad, OPQ/OPPQ/COSS.

                    3.2. Approach to the Clinical Review
               The primary evidence of effectiveness and safety of ceftobiprole for the proposed indications of
               the treatment of SAB and ABSSSI in adults, and CABP in adult and pediatric patients were
               provided in five clinical trials. Four of the trials were submitted for efficacy evaluation of
               ceftobiprole. The HABP/ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia (VABP) trial was submitted
               to support the safety evaluation. All five studies were randomized, double-blind, active-
               controlled, multicenter, phase 3 studies. The active control and the ceftobiprole dosing used in
               each study varied based on the clinical condition being treated. The endpoint evaluations in each
               trial were also adjusted based on the clinical indication. Additional data from post-marketing
               surveillance from other countries along with a review of literature publications were evaluated to
               support the safety evaluation. See Section 7.3 for further details.
               Key review issues that were identified during the review are addressed in greater detail in
               Sections 6.3 for efficacy and Section 7.7 for safety. Overall, the submitted clinical trials were
               adequate for the safety and efficacy evaluation of ceftobiprole. Table 5 provides an overview of
               the clinical trials relevant to the review of ceftobiprole’s efficacy and safety.

                    5.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential

               Nonclinical Ceftobiprole PK/PD Information
               Several studies were conducted to examine the nonclinical pharmacokinetics (PK)/
               pharmacodynamics (PD) of ceftobiprole in murine thigh and pneumonia models. Percent of time
               that free-drug concentrations remain above the minimum inhibitory concentration (%fT>MIC)
               was best correlated with ceftobiprole efficacy, indicating that antibacterial activity of
               ceftobiprole is time dependent, similar to other beta-lactams (see Section 14.1.1 for more
               information).

               Identification of PK/PD Target
               An efficacy study was performed in neutropenic thigh-infected mice given single subcutaneous
               doses (0.2 mL/ dose) of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (10, 40, and 160 mg/kg). A sigmoid
               dose-response model derived from the four-parameter Hill equation was used to calculate the
               dose of ceftobiprole producing a net bacteriostatic effect and 1-log10 kill over 24 hours. The free
               time above MIC (fT > MIC) values for each static and 1-log kill dose were estimated from PK
               and MICs. Ceftobiprole was tested against a total of 14 gram-positive strains and five strains of
               gram-negative bacteria, including E. coli, K. pneumoniae and P. aeruginosa and E. cloacae (see
               Section 14.1.1 for more information). The results of %fT > MIC to achieve bacteriostasis, 1-
               log10 kill and 2-log kill are presented in Table 7.

               The recommended dosage in pediatric subjects with CABP is outlined in Table 11. Evidence of

                                       6.2.1. SAB, Trial BPR-CS-009

                           6.2.1.1. Design, Trial BPR-CS-009
               Trial BPR-CS-009 was conducted from August 2018 to March 2022. The trial protocol was
               reviewed as a special protocol assessment (SPA) under investigational new drug application
               (IND) 64407. This was a randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled, parallel-
               arm, multi-center trial in adult hospitalized subjects with SAB, including infective endocarditis
               (IE), which was conducted in two parts. Part 1 enrolled an initial cohort of subjects (Cohort 1)
               for a maximum treatment duration of 28 days as animal studies had indicated the potential of an
               increased risk of convulsions with prolonged ceftobiprole treatment duration (> 4 weeks) and no
               prior clinical studies of ceftobiprole with this treatment duration had been conducted. Based on a
               safety evaluation of Cohort 1, the Data and Safety Monitoring Board decided that it was safe to
               proceed to Part 2. Part 2 allowed a longer treatment duration of up to 42 days and the inclusion
               of subjects with more difficult to treat infections such as osteomyelitis and epidural or cerebral
               abscess who were excluded from Cohort 1. Subjects with left-sided infective endocarditis (LIE)
               diagnosed after randomization were also permitted to continue in the trial.
               Following a screening period of up to 72 hours, subjects were randomized 1:1 to receive
               intravenous (IV) ceftobiprole or daptomycin ± aztreonam. The randomization was stratified by
               Trial site, dialysis status, and prior antibacterial treatment use within 7 days before
               randomization. Following the completion of treatment, visits were scheduled at end-of-treatment
               (EOT) (within 72 hours of the last Trial drug administration), Day 35 (± 3 days), Day 42 (± 3
               days), and at post-treatment evaluation (PTE) on Day 70 (± 5 days) post-randomization. Note
               that the Day 35 and Day 42 visits could have been active treatment periods for subjects in Part 2

               Analysis Sets
               The analysis sets defined in the trial were as follows:

               ITT Population
               All randomized subjects.

               The Safety Population
               All randomized subjects who received at least one dose of study drug.

               mITT Population
               ITT subjects who received any dose of study medication, and who had a blood culture positive
               for S. aureus at baseline.

               CE Population
               Protocol-compliant ITT subjects who complied with important aspects of the study.

               Sample Size Determination
               The sample size estimate was based on:
                    •   A point estimate for overall success of 40% in each treatment arm in the mITT
                        population
                    •   One-sided alpha level of 0.025
                    •   Power of >80%
                    •   Non-inferiority margin of 15% for the between-arm difference in the primary endpoint
               With these assumptions, enrollment of 175 subjects per treatment arm (total of 350 subjects) was
               required for the mITT population. Assuming that approximately 90% of subjects in the ITT
               population had confirmed SAB and therefore were to be included in the mITT population, it was
               necessary for 195 subjects per arm (total of 390 subjects) to be randomized and receive Trial
               treatment.

               Statistical Methods

               Primary Analysis
               The Trial was designed to determine whether ceftobiprole was non-inferior to daptomycin for the
               primary outcome measure of overall success at the PTE Visit at Day 70 (± 5 days) after
               randomization, in the mITT population. The specified NI margin was 15%.

               Reviewer Comments
               This 15% NI margin was based on 7 studies from the pre-penicillin era reporting clinical
               outcome (survival) in untreated subjects with SAB which combined suggested all-cause mortality
               (ACM) of 76% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 71%, 79%) as well as 3 studies of mortality in
               SAB subjects receiving antibacterial treatment which suggested an ACM of 16% (95% CI: 12%,
               20%). The M1 is estimated to be 51% for ACM. The protocol stated that “An estimation of M1
               for an overall success endpoint is not possible, as this was not reported in the historical studies,

               which considered survival to be success” but that “the mortality data suggest that M1 for a
               clinical/overall success outcome for SAB would similarly be very large, i.e., in the range of 50%,
               when outcomes are compared for untreated subjects and subjects who received effective
               antibacterial treatment.” The NI margin of 15% was chosen based on clinical judgement. With a
               sample size of 250–350 subjects (in the mITT population), an NI margin of 15% would allow for
               the determination of noninferiority only if the point estimate between ceftobiprole and
               daptomycin is <5%.
               The difference in the percentage of responders (i.e., subjects with overall success at PTE)
               (ceftobiprole arm minus the comparator arm) was determined, and a two-sided 95% CI for the
               difference was computed, with adjustment for actual dialysis status, and prior antibacterial
               treatment use (defined as receipt of medications within 7 days prior to randomization that were
               categorized as potentially effective systemic antibacterial treatments). Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel
               (CMH) weights were used for the stratum weight in the calculation of the CI. The non-inferiority
               hypothesis test was a one-sided hypothesis test performed at the 2.5% level of significance. If the
               lower limit of the two-sided 95% CI for the difference in response rates in the mITT population
               was greater than −15%, the noninferiority of ceftobiprole to daptomycin therapy was concluded.

               Secondary Analyses
               Secondary analyses considered the above approach for overall success assessed by the DRC at
               the EOT visit in the ITT and CE populations. All-cause mortality was assessed in the mITT and
               ITT populations and time to death was calculated using Kaplan-Meier methods. Survival rates
               (event-free probability estimates) at Day 28 and Day 70 in the ITT and mITT populations were
               provided and associated two-sided 95% CIs were calculated using the Greenwood formula. The
               hazard ratio for all-cause mortality and associated 95% CI were provided using a Cox
               proportional-hazard model, with treatment and actual stratum (dialysis status and prior
               antibacterial treatment use) as covariates. S. aureus clearance was analyzed in a similar manner
               as all-cause mortality.

                        6.2.2. ABSSSI, Trial BPR-CS-008

                         6.2.2.1. Design, Trial BPR-CS-008
               Trial BPR-CS-008 was conducted from August 2018 to March 2022. The protocol was reviewed
               as a SPA under IND 64407. The design of pivotal trial BPR-CS-008 was based on the current
               FDA Guidance for Industry Acute Bacterial Skin and Skin Structure Infections: Developing
               Drugs for Treatment, October 2013, including with respect to the efficacy endpoints, timing of
               assessments, and statistical considerations.
               This was a randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, parallel-arm, multicenter trial in adult
               hospitalized subjects to establish the safety and efficacy of ceftobiprole compared with
               vancomycin plus aztreonam in the treatment of ABSSSIs. The trial had a noninferiority design,
               with vancomycin plus aztreonam selected as an established comparator regimen. Vancomycin,
               recognized in current guidelines as the standard treatment for ABSSSI, is effective against gram-
               positive bacteria, including MRSA. Aztreonam was added to vancomycin due to its efficacy
               against gram-negative bacteria.
               Trial BPR-CS-008 was conducted in three phases:
               1. Pre-treatment: Screening and baseline, duration up to 24 hours.
               2. Active treatment: Randomization and at least 5 days, and up to 10 days, of study drug
                  administration. Study treatment could be extended up to 14 days if required.
               3. Post-treatment: An EOT visit within 24 hours after last treatment, a test-of-cure (TOC) visit
                  15 – 22 days after randomization and at least 5 days after EOT, and a last follow-up visit 28 –
                  35 days after last treatment. In addition, survival status (Alive; Dead; Lost to Follow-up) was
                  to be verified for evaluation of all-cause mortality. Survival status (by telephone or visit) was
                  to be obtained at Day 28 (± 2 days).
               The total duration of the study for each subject was approximately 5 – 7 weeks.
               The selected ceftobiprole dose was the dose approved for the HABP and CABP indications in
               non-U.S. countries: 500 mg administered as a 2-hour IV infusion every 8 hours, to be adjusted
               for subjects with moderate or severe renal impairment (500 mg of ceftobiprole is equivalent to
               667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium). The dose of vancomycin was 1,000 mg or 15 mg/kg
               administered as a 2-hour IV infusion every 12 hours; this could be modified for renal function.
               The dose of aztreonam was 1,000 mg per 0.5-hour IV infusion every 12 hours, to be adjusted for
               subjects with severe renal impairment; the need for treatment with aztreonam was to be
               reassessed at the 72-hour study Visit.

               Other design considerations:
               •    Primary measurement of the target lesion size was to be performed using a flexible ruler,
                    measuring longest length, and maximum width perpendicular to the length.
               •    Measurements were to be performed at Screening (prior to randomization and within the 6
                    hours prior to first dose of study drug), twice on Day 2, Day 3, and Day 4, and once on
                    Day 8, and the EOT, TOC, and last follow-up visits. On days when two measurements were
                    obtained, the measurements were to be taken at least 8 hours apart. Infection-site assessment
                    includes incision/drainage, erythema, heat/localized warmth, pain/tenderness to palpation,
                    fluctuance, and swelling/induration.
               •    A digital photograph was to be obtained at Screening, at the early clinical response
                    assessment (48–72 hours after first treatment), and at the EOT and TOC Visit, for each
                    subject (primary ABSSSI lesion), and was to be used for documentation purposes and as
                    source data. Digital photography was not to be used for the measurement of the ABSSSI
                    lesion size area; the determination of the ABSSSI lesion size area was to be solely based on
                    the ruler measurements.
               •    Clinical success was to be assessed by the investigator using a four-point scale relative to the
                    baseline assessment: cured, improved, stable, or worsened. In case of worsened (e.g.,
                    bacteremia, osteomyelitis, amputation), signs and symptoms needed to be documented as
                    AEs.
               •    Concomitant antibacterial therapies, other drug therapies, and non-drug procedures were to
                    be assessed at all scheduled study visits.
               •    Survival status (by telephone or visit) was to be obtained at Day 28.
               The primary objective for Trial BPR-CS-008 was to demonstrate the non-inferiority of
               ceftobiprole to vancomycin plus aztreonam in subjects with ABSSSI with respect to early
               clinical response based on percent reduction in lesion size at 48 – 72 hours after first treatment in
               the ITT population.
               The main secondary objective was to demonstrate the non-inferiority of ceftobiprole to
               vancomycin plus aztreonam in subjects with ABSSSI with respect to investigator-assessed
               clinical success at the TOC visit 15 – 22 days after randomization in the ITT and Clinically
               Evaluable populations.

               Primary Endpoint
               Early clinical response based on percent reduction from baseline in lesion size at 48 – 72 hours
               after first study-drug administration, measured in subjects who did not receive rescue therapy,
               and were alive. A clinical response was defined as a percentage reduction in lesion size greater
               than or equal to 20 percent compared to baseline.

               The Main Secondary Endpoint
               Investigator-assessed clinical success at the TOC visit 15 – 22 days after randomization, and at
               least 5 days after the EOT, assessed in the ITT and CE populations.

                            6.2.2.2. Eligibility Criteria, Trial BPR-CS-008
               The eligible subject population for trial BPR-CS-008 included adults who were diagnosed with
               ABSSSI (cellulitis/erysipelas, major cutaneous abscess, wound infection) with regional or
               systemic signs of infection, who were hospitalized (in a hospital or equivalent medical
               confinement or clinical research unit) and required IV antibacterial treatment. Subjects with
               other forms of ABSSSI or uncomplicated skin and skin structure infections were excluded, as
               were those with infections related to prosthetic devices, or infections which required more than
               two surgical interventions.
               Subjects who had received any systemic antibacterial treatment within 14 days, or topical
               antibacterial on the primary lesion within 96 hours, before first infusion of study drug, were also
               excluded.
               The minimum lesion size had to be 75 cm2 using standardized measurements (longest length of
               the lesion by widest width perpendicular to that length) with a flexible plastic ruler. The
               proportion of subjects with major cutaneous abscesses was also not to exceed 30% of the total
               subject population included.

                    c. At least two of the following local signs of infection:
                        •    erythema
                        •    induration
                        •    localized warmth
                        •    pain or tenderness on palpation
                        •    swelling/edema

               Prohibited Concomitant Medications
               Concomitant systemic antibacterial drugs were prohibited during the trial up to the TOC visit,
               with the following exceptions:
               1. Vancomycin PO 125 mg or 250 mg every 6 hours, fidaxomicin PO 200 mg q12h, or
                   metronidazole IV or PO 500 mg q8h, in both treatment arms, for the treatment of Clostridium
                   difficile infections.
               2. Metronidazole IV as adjunctive therapy in both treatment arms for coverage of anaerobic
                  bacteria.
               3. Nitrofurantoin at any time during the trial in both treatment arms as it does not achieve
                  therapeutic blood levels.
               All NSAIDs were prohibited until 72 hours after start of treatment, and were then permitted only
               after early clinical response had been determined.
               The administration of steroids (>40 mg per day prednisolone, or equivalent), or
               immunosuppressants was prohibited between administration of first study drug and the TOC
               Visit.
               Chronic systemic therapy with calcineurin-inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus, or cyclosporin),
               mycophenolate mofetil or mycophenolate sodium, azathioprine, sirolimus, and topical
               antibacterial drugs on the primary lesion was prohibited from randomization to the TOC Visit.

               Non-Drug Adjunctive Therapy
               Adjuvant surgical treatment was recognized as appropriate and necessary for adequate treatment
               of wound infections and abscesses. Subjects were evaluated at Screening to determine whether
               more than one intra-operative surgical intervention was required. Those expected to require more
               than two surgical interventions in the operating room for the ABSSSI were to be excluded from
               the trial.
               When indicated, the initial surgical procedure was to be performed before randomization, and
               subsequent procedures performed no later than 48 hours after the start of treatment.
               Adjunctive therapies permitted for the treatment of ABSSSI at any time were debridement at the
               bedside, topical solutions, including antiseptic agents such as povidone-iodine (topical solutions
               did not contain anti-microbial agents), and local bedside wound care in accordance with hospital
               protocols.

               Analysis Populations

               The ITT Population
               Included all randomized subjects, analyzed according to the treatment they were randomized to
               receive, and if different, not according to what they actually received.

               The Microbiological ITT Population
               Was the subset of subjects in the ITT population who had causative (i.e., infecting) pathogens
               identified by the central microbiology laboratory from skin lesion or blood cultures; local
               laboratory identification results were only used if the corresponding causative pathogen was not
               available for identification by the central laboratory. Subjects with no pathogens isolated at
               Baseline (microbiologically non-evaluable) were excluded from the microbiological ITT (micro-
               ITT) population.

               CE Population
               Was the subset of subjects in the ITT population who complied with important aspects of the
               trial until the TOC visit, i.e., with no major protocol deviations (e.g., a completed response
               outcome assessment, and no concomitant systemic antibacterial treatment or topical antibacterial
               applied to the primary lesion).

               The Microbiologically Evaluable Population
               Was the subset of subjects in the micro-ITT population who were also in the CE population.
               Analysis at each time point was performed on subjects with available response at that time point
               (excluding those with microbiological response of ‘Not Evaluable’ or missing).

               Sample Size Determination
               A sample size of 674 subjects (337 per arm) provided at least 90% power to reject the
               null hypothesis (H0) against the alternative hypothesis (HA) at the one-sided alpha level of
               0.025 as follows, using a two-arm large-sample normal approximation test of Proportions.
               Early clinical response rates of an at least 20% reduction in lesion area size (primary
               endpoint) and clinical cure rates at the TOC visit (main secondary endpoint) were based on
               recent phase 3 studies in ABSSSI. The sample size estimate was based on a point estimate for
               early clinical response of 80% in each treatment arm in the ITT and CE population, a one-sided
               alpha level of 0.025, a non-inferiority margin of 10 percentage points for the between-arm
               difference of the primary endpoint.

               Data Monitoring and Interim Analyses
               Investigators, Applicant employees, and others involved in the conduct and analysis of the Trial
               (with the exception of the unblinded pharmacist or delegate) remained blinded to the treatment
               codes and interim analysis results until all monitoring decisions were made, and the database
               locked for the final analysis.

               A blinded interim analysis for sample size re-estimation assessed whether the initial sample size
               estimate was adequate for evaluating the primary endpoint, and to select a larger sample size if
               warranted.

               Statistical Methods
               Trial BPR-CS-008 was designed to determine whether ceftobiprole was non-inferior to
               vancomycin plus aztreonam for both the primary endpoint of early clinical response and the main
               secondary endpoint of investigator-assessed clinical success at the TOC visit. The main primary
               analysis was based on the ITT population consisting of all randomized subjects. The weighted
               difference in percentage of responders at 48–72 h (ceftobiprole arm minus the vancomycin plus
               aztreonam arm), and the 95% CI for the weighted difference was computed using CMH weights
               method adjusted for geographical region (North America and Europe), and actual type of
               ABSSSI.
               The non-inferiority hypothesis test was a one-sided hypothesis test performed at the 2.5% level
               of significance. If the lower limit of the two-sided 95% CI for the difference in response rates
               (ceftobiprole minus vancomycin plus aztreonam) in the ITT population was greater than -10%,
               the non-inferiority of ceftobiprole to vancomycin plus aztreonam would be concluded. If non-
               inferiority was declared at the one-sided significance level of 0.025, then the difference would be
               tested for superiority. Superiority would be declared if the lower limit of the two-sided 95% CI
               exceeded 0 (or equivalently p-value less than 0.05 using CMH test). The same analysis was
               repeated on the CE population.

               Reviewer Comments
               The overall data from two studies by Snodgrass in 1937, both of which compared ultraviolet
               light against a sulfonamide antibacterial drug, in subjects with cellulitis/erysipelas for an
               outcome of cessation of spread of lesion at 48-72 hours, support a treatment difference of 18%.
               Because this is thought to be conservatively estimated at 18 percent for antibacterial drugs in the
               treatment of ABSSSI for the endpoint based on lesion size assessment, further discounting of the
               treatment effect may not be necessary and thus M1 is estimated to be 18 percent. These scientific
               data provide support for the selection of a noninferiority margin of 10 percent that preserves
               some of M1 based on an endpoint of lesion size assessment. Refer to the ABSSSI Guidance2 for
               further details on the justification of a 10% NI margin for ABSSSI.
               The main secondary analysis was based on the weighted difference in percentage of clinical
               success at the TOC visit (ceftobiprole arm minus the vancomycin plus aztreonam arm), and the

               Primary Analysis
               As shown in Table 27, ceftobiprole met the primary objective of this trial by demonstrating the
               non-inferiority of ceftobiprole (greater than the pre-specified 10% non-inferiority margin) to
               vancomycin plus aztreonam for the primary endpoint of early clinical response based on a 20%
               or more reduction from baseline in lesion size at 48–72 hours after start of trial drug
               administration. In the ITT population (primary analysis population), 306 subjects (91.3%) in the
               ceftobiprole arm were responders (95% CI: 87.8, 94.1) versus 303 (88.1%) subjects in the
               vancomycin plus aztreonam arm (95% CI: 84.2, 91.3). The proportion difference (ceftobiprole
               minus vancomycin plus aztreonam) was 3.3% (95% CI: −1.2, 7.8). Since −1.2% (the lower limit
               of this 95% CI) exceeded the required NI limit of −10%, non-inferiority was demonstrated.
               There were 29 (8.7%) and 41 (11.9%) non-responders in the ceftobiprole and vancomycin plus
               aztreonam arms, respectively. The most common reason for non-responders at 48-72 hours after
               start of treatment was <20% reduction from baseline in surface area of primary lesion which
               included 65.5% of ceftobiprole non-responders and 70.7% of vancomycin plus aztreonam non-
               responders. In general, there were no notable treatment differences regarding the reasons for
               non-response.

                         6.2.3. CABP, Trial CAP-3001

                           6.2.3.1. Design, Trial CAP-3001
               This was a randomized, double-blind, multicenter trial of ceftobiprole versus ceftriaxone with or
               without linezolid designed to assess the efficacy and safety of ceftobiprole in adult subjects with
               CABP requiring hospitalization. The trial was conducted from June 2006 to July 2007.


                                                                                                                                                 91



Reference ID: 5357793

               NDA 218275
               Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
               The primary objective of this trial was to demonstrate the noninferiority of ceftobiprole
               compared with ceftriaxone with or without linezolid with respect to the clinical cure rate at the
               TOC visit in subjects hospitalized with CABP.
               The secondary objectives were to compare the following in hospitalized CABP subjects after
               treatment with ceftobiprole versus treatment with the comparator:
               •    The microbiological eradication rate at the TOC Visit
               •    The clinical cure rate and the microbiological eradication rate at the TOC Visit of subjects
                    who required mechanical ventilation within the first 48 hours of enrollment
               •    The clinical and microbiological relapse rates at the late follow-up visit
               •    The 30-day pneumonia-specific mortality rates.
               Since many subjects in this trial would not require hospitalization for the entire duration of
               antibacterial therapy, a switch from IV study drugs to oral cefuroxime axetil (500 mg every
               12 hours) was allowed after a minimum of 3 days of IV therapy, but only for those subjects who
               met all protocol-specified criteria for improvement and were candidates for hospital discharge.

               Sample Size Determination
               The sample size was determined to show the noninferiority of ceftobiprole compared with
               ceftriaxone with or without linezolid in terms of the clinical cure rate at the TOC visit.
               The sample size calculation was based on the following assumptions for the ITT analysis set:
               •    The clinical cure rate is 70% in both treatment arms,
               •    The non-inferiority margin is 10%,
               •    The power (1-β) is 80%,
               •    The level of significance is 2-sided 5%,
               •    The clinically evaluable rate is 80%.
               Based on the above, 670 subjects needed to be randomly assigned to treatment, providing 335
               subjects in each treatment arm.

               Efficacy Analysis Sets
               •    ITT Analysis Set: included all subjects randomly assigned to treatment.
               •    mITT Analysis Set: a subset of the ITT analysis set that included all ITT subjects who had a
                    valid pathogen at Baseline.
               •    Clinically Evaluable Analysis Set: a subset of the ITT analysis set that included all the ITT
                    subjects who received at least 48 hours of Trial medication but excluded those subjects with
                    a derived clinical outcome of Not Evaluable at the TOC Visit. The derived clinical outcome
                    was based on clinical assessment and evaluability of a subject, whereas the clinical outcome
                    collected in the electronic case report form was based on the investigator’s assessment.
               •    Clinically Evaluable Analysis Set at the Late Follow-Up Visit: included all clinically
                    evaluable subjects with a derived clinical outcome of cure at the TOC visit and who were
                    clinically evaluable at the late follow-up visit.
               •    Microbiologically Evaluable Analysis Set: a subset of the mITT analysis set that included
                    all mITT subjects who were also clinically evaluable subjects, excluding those with a
                    microbiological outcome of ‘Not Evaluable’ at the TOC Visit.
               •    Microbiologically Evaluable Analysis Set at the Late Follow-Up Visit: included all
                    microbiologically evaluable subjects with a microbiological outcome of eradication or
                    presumed eradication at the TOC visit and who were microbiologically evaluable at the late
                    follow-up visit.
               •    Safety Analysis Set: The safety analysis set is a subset of the ITT analysis set and included
                    all the subjects in the ITT analysis set who were exposed to any Trial medication.

               ‘Not Evaluable’ by the investigator were considered failures. Subjects who were considered

               A subject was considered a ‘derived clinical cure’ at the TOC visit if the clinical outcome at the

               Evaluability at the TOC Visit
               A subject was deemed clinically evaluable at the TOC visit unless he or she met any of the
               following criteria:

               • Mortality:
                    Early Mortality: The subject died within 48 hours after the first infusion.
                    Unrelated Mortality: The mortality was unrelated to pneumonia and the last clinical
                        assessment was not worsened, and the subject had no treatment-related adverse event, did
                        not withdraw due to lack of efficacy, and had no TOC visit.
                    Effective Concomitant Therapy: The subject took a systemic antibacterial drug
                        (administered for a reason other than CABP), against gram-positive or gram-negative
                        pathogens. Subjects who received a concomitant medication with purely anaerobic (e.g.,
                        metronidazole), anti-fungal, or antiviral activity were considered evaluable. Subjects who
                        received non-absorbable antibacterial drugs s (e.g., oral vancomycin, neomycin) or
                        topical antibacterial drugs were also evaluable.

                            laboratory results.
               •    Inappropriate Clinical Evaluation:

                      to 21 days following the last dose of study drug.
               •    Course Too Short:
                     The subject took study medication for less than 48 hours, or
                     The subject had a clinical outcome of ‘Cure’ at the TOC visit but took study medication
                      for less than 120 hours, or
