               Conclusion of the Review of Impurities not Fully Qualified in Toxicology Studies
               The impurity qualification review indicates that the select individual impurities in the DS and DP
               are not adequately qualified based on the toxicology studies considered. However, the levels of
               these impurities in ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for the intended clinical treatment durations
               and indications are considered acceptable based on the following considerations: 1) The
               impurities specified below share significant structural similarities with ceftobiprole medocaril
               sodium and represent a small fraction of the DP, therefore, these individual impurities are not
               likely to cause greater toxicities than those observed with exposure to the DP. 2) The overall
               analysis of the mutagenic potential of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (prodrug), which shares
               similar structural alerts with the individual impurities evaluated, indicates that ceftobiprole
               medocaril sodium and associated impurities are not likely to have mutagenic potential. 3)
               Although mixed results have been observed with ceftobiprole medocaril sodium and ceftobiprole
               in in vitro mutagenicity tests (negative in a limited Ames test, positive in the mouse lymphoma
               assay, but negative in a more recent HPRT forward mutation assay), primarily associated with

               QSAR state of the art models: Derek Nexus six 6.3.0 (DX), Leadscope Model Applier 2022.0.2.3

                        14.1.1. Preclinical Studies to Determine the PK/PD
                             Target of Ceftobiprole
               Identification of PK/PD Index
               The percentage of time during a dosing interval when the unbound drug concentration exceeds
               the minimum inhibitory concentration (%fT>MIC) has been identified as the PK/PD index that
               best correlates with the bactericidal activity of most β-lactam drugs.
               Dose fractionation studies conducted with S. aureus American type culture collection (ATCC)
               33591 confirmed the PK/PD index best correlated with in vivo efficacy was %fT > MIC (Figure
               23).

               Identification of PK/PD Target
               The activity of ceftobiprole was evaluated in a mouse neutropenic thigh-infection model. Mice
               were given single subcutaneous doses (0.2 mL/ dose) of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (10, 40,
               and 160 mg/kg). A sigmoid dose-response model derived from the four-parameter Hill equation
               was used to calculate the dose of ceftobiprole producing a net bacteriostatic effect and 1-log10
               kill over 24 hours. The %fT > MIC values for each static and 1-log kill dose were estimated from
               PK and MICs. Ceftobiprole was tested against a total of 14 gram-positive strains (n = 8 S. aureus
               and n = 6 S. pneumoniae) and five strains of gram-negative bacteria, including E. coli, K.
               pneumoniae, P. aeruginosa, and E. cloacae. The results of %fT > MIC to achieve net bacterial
               stasis, 1-log10 kill and 2-log kill are presented in Table 197.
               Since free-drug plasma %fT>MIC targets from this study were only reported for net bacterial
               stasis and a 2-log10 colony forming unit (CFU) reduction from baseline, free-drug plasma
               %fT>MIC targets associated with a 1-log10 CFU reduction from baseline were linearly
               interpolated by averaging the targets for net bacterial stasis and a 2-log10 CFU reduction from
               Baseline.
               Overall, these pharmacodynamics studies suggested that bactericidal (1-log kill) %fT>MIC
               values of approximately 30% and 50% would provide efficacious dosing for ceftobiprole for
               treatment of infections caused by gram-positive and gram-negative pathogens, respectively.

                        14.1.2. Protein Binding
               Initial studies investigated the plasma protein binding of ceftobiprole by ultrafiltration in mouse,
               rat, rabbit, dog, marmoset, Cynomolgus monkey, and human (BAP00112, BAP00566). Results
               from both studies indicated that plasma protein binding was low, ranging from approximately
               10% to 45% across species, and independent of drug concentrations (10 or 100 μg/mL). In
               humans, plasma protein binding ranged from 22.1% to 40.8%. These initial studies used a small
               sample size and showed a high intra- and inter-experimental variability for human plasma
               protein binding.

               Table 201. Plasma Protein Binding of Ceftobiprole in Animal Species and Human




               Source: Study BAP00556; Study BAP00112


               Due to the variability noted in studies BAP00112 and BAP00566, two additional studies were
               conducted to investigate human plasma protein binding. The first study utilized ultrafiltration to
               investigate ceftobiprole binding to human plasma protein (FK5789). Protein binding was
               measured at concentrations ranging from 0.5 to 100 μg/mL in pooled plasma samples from male
               and female healthy normal volunteers. Results indicated that plasma protein binding was low and
               concentration independent, with the mean percent binding equaling 17.3%.
               A second study (FK6157) was conducted to confirm the extent of plasma protein binding
               observed, due to differences noted in the later study versus the preliminary studies. The study
               used freshly obtained (i.e., within 72 hours), non-pooled human plasma samples, which were
               incubated with ceftobiprole at concentrations of 3.5 and 35 μg/mL. Results again indicated that
               plasma protein binding was low and concentration independent, with a mean percent binding of
               15.4%.

                        14.1.3. Metabolism
               Conversion of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium to ceftobiprole is very rapid in human plasma (38
               seconds; study BAP00072). Inhibition studies with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid suggested
               that type A plasma esterases are involved in the cleavage of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium to
               ceftobiprole (study BAP00207). A mechanistic study investigating the enzymes involved in the
               hydrolysis of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium demonstrated a lack of specificity of this conversion
               which occurred both enzymatically (by paraoxonases and other hydrolytic enzymes) and non-
               enzymatically (Study FK6700).
               In vitro hepatocyte studies indicated the primary metabolite is the open-ring hydrolysis product
               (study BAP00070). The prodrug ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is rapidly hydrolyzed, in contrast
               to the active moiety ceftobiprole, which is slowly metabolized. At least three additional,
               unidentified metabolites were present in trace amounts. Thus, ceftobiprole does not appear to be
               a substrate of CYP enzymes. The proposed metabolism of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is
               presented in Figure 24.

                        14.1.4. Potential for CYP Enzyme-Mediated Drug-Drug
                             Interactions
               No clinical drug-drug interaction studies of ceftobiprole have been performed.
               In vitro CYP inhibition data (ceftobiprole concentration up to 200 μM; 107 μg/mL) are
               summarized in Table 203. Only a slight (6% to 28%) inhibitory potential was apparent in the
               highest concentration range tested (50 to 200 μM; 26.7 to 107 μg/mL; 1009572, FK6366, and
               FK6604). Ceftobiprole was not a time-dependent inhibitor of prototypical CYP substrates at the
               highest concentrations tested (200 μM; 107 μg/mL; studies FK6366 and FK6604). Due to
               solubility constraints, subsequent attempts to evaluate the direct and metabolism-dependent in
               vitro inhibition of human CYP enzymes at higher concentrations of ceftobiprole were

                             Interactions
               Ceftobiprole as a Substrate Of P-Glycoprotein and Breast Cancer Resistance Protein
               In vitro experiments were conducted to determine whether ceftobiprole is a substrate of drug
               (efflux) transporters P-gp and breast cancer resistance protein in a bidirectional permeability
               assay across MDCKII cells (studies FK5942, XT138008, and XT228043). The bi-directional
               permeability of ceftobiprole (1, 10, and 100 μM; 0.535, 7.14, and 53.5 μg/mL) across MDCKII-
               MDR1, MDCKII-BCRP and control cells was low at all conditions (less than 3 x 10-6 cm/sec,
               similar to the control). The net efflux ratio of ceftobiprole was ≤2 at all concentrations and on all
               cell lines suggesting that ceftobiprole is not a substrate of either P-gp or BCRP.

                        14.2.5. Drug Penetration
               Soft Tissue Penetration
               CSI-1002 was an exploratory study to evaluate the penetration of ceftobiprole into soft tissue
               determined by in vivo microdialysis in healthy subjects.
               This Study was conducted in two sequential parts: a pilot study and a main study. The pilot study
               was conducted in 3 control subjects. Ceftobiprole was locally administered via microdialysis
               followed by a washout period of 3 hours during which dialysate samples were taken every
               30 minutes for 4 hours.
               The main study was conducted in 12 healthy subjects. Ceftobiprole was administered locally via
               microdialysis followed by a washout period of 3 hours. After the washout period, each subject
               received a single 2-hour IV infusion of 500 mg ceftobiprole medocaril sodium. Dialysate
               samples were collected pre-dose and every 20 min from start of infusion through 12 hours post-
               start of dosing. Blood samples were collected at time 0 (pre-dose) up to 24 hours after the start of
               the infusion.
               Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium concentrations were only assessed in plasma. Protein binding in
               plasma was determined by ultra-filtration at pre-dose, 2, and 12 hours after the start of the
               infusion. Concentrations of ceftobiprole in dialysate were quantified using a validated high-
               performance liquid chromatography/ultraviolet method.

               Base Model
               The final base model was a 3-compartment PK model with linear elimination from the central
               compartment, and baseline creatinine clearance (CLcr) was included on CL a priori. Additive
               error models (in the log domain) were separate for phase 1 and phase 3 studies. The model
               structure is shown in Figure 26.
               Interindividual variability (IIV) was modelled assuming a log-normal distribution for patient
               level random effects. Residual variability was tested as additive, proportional, or combined.
               Model evaluation and selection of the base model were based on standard statistical criteria of
               goodness-of-fit (GoF) such as a decrease in the minimum objective function value (OFV),
               accuracy of parameter estimation (i.e., 95% confidence interval excluding 0), successful model
               convergence, and diagnostic plots.

               Reviewer Comments
               The reviewer was able to reproduce the Applicant’s refined PopPK model for SAB (i.e., final
               model). The final parameter estimates were precise (all %SEM under 13.3% except CL shift for
               SAB was moderate at 36.7%) and aligned with the resampled parameter estimates (90%
               confidence interval [CI] contains model parameter estimates). Similar to the final PopPK model
               for ABSSSI and CABP, there is no obvious bias or misspecification observed in the GoF plots
               (observed vs. predicted concentrations show good agreements and mostly align with the line of
               unity; the CWRES scatter around y = 0 without obvious trends). The NPDE and prediction-
               corrected VPC plots show that the refined SAB PopPK model can capture the observed data;
               however, when the prediction-corrected VPC plot is limited to SAB subjects, some under-
               predictions are shown and are more prominent beyond 8 hours. This is likely due to the
               relatively sparse PK available in the 8-to-24-hour timeframe (based on time from last dose).
               Overall, the model reasonably captures central tendency of the SAB PK data. The Applicant’s
               final SAB model is acceptable in describing ceftobiprole disposition, in deriving exposure
               metrics for exposure-response analysis for the SAB population, and in simulating for target
               attainment analysis (i.e., PTA) in adult subjects with SAB.
               In the phase 3 trial in SAB subjects, a total of 21 subjects with ESRD were randomized to
               continue iHD renal replacement modality while receiving ceftobiprole (n=20 in the final
               NONMEM dataset); however, the reviewer noted in the Applicant’s report that, “the exact times
               at which hemodialysis was started and stopped was not recorded, the trial protocol stipulated

               Base Model
               The original PopPK model structure was fitted to the pooled pediatric and adult dataset. The final
               base model (from pediatric data alone) was a linear 3-compartment with a direct relationship
               between renal clearance (CL) and GFR based on Rhodin and fat-free mass (GFRRhodin, FFM). Body
               weight was included on volume (estimated exponent) and clearance related terms (fixed
               exponent of 0.75). IIV was included on central volume of distribution (Vc) only.
               For the final base model, IIV was modelled assuming a log-normal distribution for subject level
               random effects. Residual variability was tested as additive, proportional, or combined. Model
               evaluation and selection of the base model were based on standard statistical criteria of GoF such
               as a decrease in the OFV, accuracy of parameter estimation (i.e., 95% confidence interval
               excluding 0), successful model convergence, and diagnostic plots.

               Covariate Model

                         14.5.2.2. Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia PK/PD Analysis

                               14.5.2.2.1. Introduction
               The Applicant performed PK/PD analyses for the SAB populations with the following objects:
               •    To evaluate exposure-efficacy relationships using the refined PopPK model for SAB
               •    To conduct PTA to support ceftobiprole dosing regimens and susceptibility testing
                    interpretive criteria against S. aureus

                               14.5.2.2.2. Exposure-Efficacy Analysis
               Exposure-efficacy relationship was evaluated for SAB using PK and clinical data from Trial
               BPR-CS-008. Dosing regimens administered in SAB subjects are summarized in Table 262. The
               primary endpoint was overall success in the treatment of SAB, including infective endocarditis,
               at the post-treatment evaluation (PTE) visit (Day 70 +/- 5 post-randomization) in the mITT
               population (defined as the subset of subjects in the intent-to-treat (ITT) population who received
               any amount of study medication, and who had a blood culture positive for S. aureus at baseline
               based on a central microbiology laboratory assessment). Overall success is defined if the
               following criteria were met:
               •    Subject was alive at PTE visit;
               •    No new metastatic foci or complications of the SAB infection;
               •    Resolution or improvement of SAB-related clinical signs and symptoms; and
               •    Two negative blood cultures for S. aureus
               •    At least one while subject was on active study treatment, and
               •    confirmed by at least one subsequent negative blood culture for S. aureus (either in the
                    period between 7 days after the end-of-treatment (EOT) visit and PTE visit or at the PTE
                    visit)
               The Applicant employed two analysis populations for the exposure-efficacy analysis: 1) mITT
               population with baseline pathogen, microbiological data, and sufficient PK data and 2) a
               subpopulation of the first analysis population with S. aureus isolated at baseline. A total of 174
               and 172 subjects were included in the mITT and mITT S. aureus analysis populations,
               respectively. Refer to the Applicant’s PK/PD report (Tables 10 and 11 in the submitted report)
               for a summary of baseline characteristics of the analysis populations. The response for efficacy
               endpoints by visits in two analysis populations are summarized in Table 263. Ceftobiprole MIC,
               free-drug AUC, and Day 1 free-drug plasma %T>MIC for both analysis populations are
               summarized in Table 264. Percent of subjects in each analysis population achieving nonclinical
               targets is summarized in Table 265. Given that individual %T>MIC aggregate at the high end of
               respective ranges, the exposure-efficacy analyses (univariable or multivariable) were not
               performed by the Applicant.
               Of note, two subjects had A. baumannii and C. striatum selected as baseline pathogens with
               MICs of >64 and >16 µg/mL, respectively. For these two subjects, the free-drug %T>MIC were
               of 0% on Days 1 and 10 and were categorized as failures regarding overall success endpoints at
               EOT and PTE. While the free-drug plasma %T>MIC with respect to the baseline S. aureus

                           14.5.2.3. Assessment of End-Stage Renal Disease Dosing
                                  Regimen for Adults
               For adult subjects with ESRD (on or not on iHD), 250 mg IV q24h is the recommended dosing
               regimen (for all indications); however, model-based simulations show that the
               exposure (i.e., Day 1 AUC) may be suboptimal in ESRD subjects (not on iHD) with
               renal function of 0-15 mL/min when compared to those with normal renal function (defined as
               90-150 mL/min) in ABSSSI (Figure 45). Numerically lower model-predicted exposures on Day
               1 are also seen with CABP and SAB infection types. As such, an Information Request was
               communicated to the Applicant to compare ESRD dosing (not on iHD) at q12h vs. q24h dosing
               frequencies and provide safety assessment for the q12h dosing regimen.
               While the q12h dosing may seem reasonable based on Day 1 exposure metrics, the exposures
               (after multiple-day administrations) on Day 5 for SAB and Day 7 for ABSSSI and CABP are
               higher than those observed to date in clinical and nonclinical studies (Table 275). Additionally,
               the Applicant stated that there has been no clinical safety experience at the predicted exposures
               that would be reached based on the q12h dosing regimen in ESRD subjects.

                           14.5.2.5. Assessment of Severe Renal Impairment Dosing
                                  Regimen for Adolescents
               Based on the submitted PK/PD report for pediatric subjects for the CABP indication (Report
               00616-3), a dose of 7.5 mg/kg q24h (up to 500 mg) was recommended for adolescents 12 to
               <18 years of age; however, the Applicant proposes the same weight-based dosing at q12h dosing
               frequency (i.e., 7.5 mg/kg q12h, up to 250 mg) in the severe RI category. As such, an
               Information Request (dated 5 FEBRUARY 2024; link) was communicated to the Applicant.
               Briefly, the Applicant stated that the decision to modify from q24h to q12h was to align with
               adult dosing regimen for severe RI through interactions with the European Health Authorities.
               Additionally, the Applicant provided further simulations to support the q12h dosing regimen in
               this population as summarized in Table 282. At a dosing frequency of q12h (capped at 250 mg
               per dose), the exposures based on AUC would be slightly higher and the Cmax slightly lower in
               adolescent subjects with severe RI (AUC = 259 μg*h/mL; Cmax = 20.7 μg/mL) than the
               exposures predicted in subjects with q24h dosing frequency (AUC = 240 μg*h/mL; Cmax = 24.6
               μg/mL). Overall, the change in dosing frequency results in an improvement in PTA results.

               17. Clinical Safety

                        17.1. Phase 1 Studies
               The Applicant submitted eighteen adult phase 1 and two pediatric phase 1 studies for
               ceftobiprole. The population of these studies include healthy subjects, subjects on hemodialysis,
               subjects with impaired renal function and end-stage renal disease, morbidly obese subjects,
               subjects who underwent elective hip replacement surgery, and subjects who were hospitalized in
               intensive or intermediate care units. These studies covered a dose range of 125 mg to 1000 mg.
               There were no deaths in the phase 1 healthy adult studies. However, there were two adult
               subjects in the intensive care unit phase 1 studies who died due to the unrelated adverse events
               (AEs) of septic shock and intracranial hemorrhage. SAEs were reported for eight subjects (none
               in healthy adults). The only SAE which was considered related to the study drug was acute
               kidney injury. The most common AEs experienced in this population were nausea (29.6%), taste
               disorder (21%), headache (16.6%), and vomiting (11.2%). Additional AEs that occurred in >2 %
               of the subjects include dysgeusia, infusion site pain, diarrhea, hypotension, abdominal pain,
               nasopharyngitis, feeling hot, phlebitis, pyrexia, constipation, dizziness, fatigue, and injection site
               pain. The AEs experienced in phase 1 studies were similar to the AEs seen in the subsequent
               phase 3 studies. There are no significant safety issues or concerns based on the phase 1 data.

               The pediatric phase 1 studies BPR-PIP-001 and CSI-1006 were multicenter, open-label, single-
               dose, add-on studies of ceftobiprole in pediatric subjects undergoing treatment with IV
               antibacterial drugs with the aim of evaluating the single-dose PK and safety of ceftobiprole. Trial
               BPR-PIP-001 included 15 neonates and infants aged up to 3 months; 6 treatment-emergent
               adverse events (TEAEs) occurred in 6 subjects and only one TEAE of diaper dermatitis occurred
               in more than one subject. Neither the TEAEs nor the two SAEs of cerebral infarction and
               diaphragmatic hernia were considered to be related to the study drug. Study CSI-1006 included
               64 subjects aged 3 months to less than 18 years. Eight subjects experienced 14 SAEs, none of
               which were considered treatment-related by the investigator. TEAEs were reported in 48.4% of
               subjects and vomiting was the most common (9.4%). TEAEs of vomiting, diaper dermatitis,
               pruritis, headache, increased eosinophil count, diarrhea, catheter-related site reaction, urine
               crystals, increased alanine aminotransferase (125 U/L), and increased aspartate aminotransferase
               (121 U/L) were considered potentially related to ceftobiprole; the latter two laboratory-based
               TEAEs occurred in the same subject. No deaths were reported and no subjects discontinued
               either Study due to a TEAE.

               19. Clinical Microbiology

                    19.1. In Vitro Activity
               The in vitro ceftobiprole MIC range and concentrations required to inhibit 90% of isolates
               (MIC90) against the target pathogen isolates collected in the JMI SENTRY surveillance studies
               from 2016 to 2020 and isolates collected in the European Union surveillance studies from 2016
               to 2019 is shown in Table 288. Ceftobiprole is active against MSSA (MIC90 = 0.5 mcg/mL),
               MRSA (MIC90 = 2 mcg/mL), S. pneumoniae (MIC90 = 0.25-0.5 mcg/mL), S. pyogenes
               (MIC90 = 0.015 mcg/mL), S. agalactiae (MIC90 = 0.03 mcg/mL), H. influenzae (MIC90 =
               0.12 mcg/mL), and H. parainfluenzae (MIC90 = 0.25 mcg/mL). The ceftobiprole MIC90s for the
               penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae subset was higher (MIC90 = 0.5 mcg/mL) than for the
               penicillin-susceptible subset (MIC90 = 0.015 mcg/mL) but were within the proposed susceptible
               breakpoint of ≤0.5 mcg/mL for ceftobiprole.
               The ceftobiprole MIC90 for E. faecalis and E. faecium were 2 mcg/mL and >4 mcg/mL,
               respectively. The ceftobiprole MIC90 against M. catarrhalis was 0.25 mcg/mL. Against 12
               vancomycin-resistant/ampicillin-susceptible E. faecalis, the ceftobiprole MIC90 was 2 mcg/mL.
               Ceftobiprole is active against some gram-negative bacteria producing AmpC cephalosporinases
               or non-ESBL Class A enzymes with MIC90 values of ≤1 mcg/mL. Ceftobiprole has limited
               activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter species with MIC90 values of
               ≥16 mcg/mL. The ceftobiprole MIC90 values against P. aeruginosa are above the PK-PD
               target achievable by proposed dosing regimen. Ceftobiprole is not active against ESBL or
               metallo -lactamases producing bacteria. The ceftobiprole MIC90s for key pathogens, S. aureus,
               S. pneumoniae, E. coli, and K. pneumoniae isolates from the European Union surveillance were
               similar to that observed for the US isolates. Ceftobiprole, like other cephalosporins, is not active

                    19.2. Interaction With Other Antimicrobials
               In the in vitro checkboard broth and/or time kill assays, ceftobiprole was tested in combination
               with daptomycin, vancomycin, gentamicin, or rifampin against 20 MRSA strains with varying
               degrees of vancomycin susceptibility. Ceftobiprole was also tested in combination with
               doripenem, levofloxacin or colistin against strains of P. aeruginosa (N = 24), A. baumannii
               (N = 19) or fluoroquinolone-resistant E. coli (N = 19). Ceftobiprole in combination with
               ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, amikacin, and tobramycin was evaluated in 61 clinical P. aeruginosa
               isolates. No antagonism was observed in these studies. Majority of the combination were
               indifferent.


                    19.3. In Vivo Activity
               The in vivo activity of ceftobiprole was evaluated in multiple animal models of infection. These
               include the murine septicemia model, the murine peritonitis model, the neutropenic thigh
               infection model (PK-PD studies), the murine acute pneumonia model, the rat and rabbit
               endocarditis model, the rabbit meningitis model, the rat and rabbit osteomyelitis model, and the
               murine urinary tract infection model.

               Murine Septicemia Model
               Ceftobiprole (ED50 values <5 mg/kg) was effective in treating experimental septicemia in mice
               due to S. aureus strains (ceftobiprole MIC values ≤2 mcg/mL) (Table 290). Against MRSA I-6
               and MRSA 8525, ceftobiprole was more active than vancomycin (vancomycin ED50 = 6.7 mg/kg
               and 12.1 mg/kg). Ceftobiprole also demonstrated activity against three penicillin-resistant strains
               of S. pneumoniae, including a strain S. pneumoniae 23 F-CTR (ceftobiprole MIC 1 mg/mL),
               however, the ceftobiprole ED50 for the S. pneumoniae penicillin resistant strains were higher than
               the S. pneumoniae penicillin sensitive strain. Similar ceftobiprole doses (ED50 <5 mg/kg) were
               effective against E. coli, K. pneumoniae, C. freundii, S. marcescens and P. mirabilis. Against the
               TEM-1 containing E. coli OC4367, the ceftobiprole ED50 was higher (2.7 mg/kg/day) than
               against the parent E. coli strain (0.5 mg/kg/day) but ceftobiprole was more active than
               ceftazidime or cefepime and as active as meropenem. The presence of the ACT-1 AmpC
               cephalosporinase did not affect the in vivo activity of the ceftobiprole and comparators in this
               animal model. The strain Proteus vulgaris 1028 with in vitro resistance to ceftobiprole was also
               resistant in vivo (ED50 >12 mg/kg). Cefepime (ED50 = 1 mg/kg) and meropenem (ED50
               <0.4 mg/kg) had greater activity against the P. aeruginosa BA strain compared to ceftobiprole
               (ED50 = 4 mg/kg).

               Murine Acute Pneumonia Model
               In the immunocompromised murine model of acute pneumonia, the ten-day cumulative survival rates for infected mice (all strains)
               receiving ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (total daily doses of ceftobiprole equivalents, 2.1 to 75 mg/kg) ranged from 57 to 100%,
               whereas with ceftriaxone (total daily doses, 10 to 400 mg/kg), the survival rates varied between 13 and 100% (Table 292). In the
               immunocompetent murine model of acute pneumonia, ceftobiprole medocaril sodium reduced bacterial burden in the lungs. Against
               the wildtype strain ATCC 6301, and the two macrolide-resistant isolates, the ceftobiprole ED50 was 2.5- to 4-fold lower than that
               determined for ceftriaxone. Against H. influenzae, E. cloacae and the non-ESBL producing K. pneumoniae ceftobiprole, ceftriaxone
               and cefepime all reduced bacterial burden in the lungs compared to no treatment. The reason for the activity of ceftriaxone
               (MIC=16 mcg/mL; Intermediate susceptibility) against the non-ESBL producing K. pneumoniae is not clear. For the ESBL-positive K.
               pneumoniae strain where the MICs were all greater than or equal to 128 mcg/mL, there was no difference between treated and
               untreated animals. Emergence of resistance studies conducted on bacteria recovered after therapy (except for ESBL-positive K.
               pneumoniae) found post-treatment MIC values within 2-fold of pre-treatment MIC values.

               Rat and Rabbit Osteomyelitis Model
               In the rat model of MRSA mediastinitis and sternal osteomyelitis (Table 294), ceftobiprole (70
               and 100 mg/kg for 5 days) decreased the MRSA load in the sternum by 1 log10 and 1.4 log10
               compared with untreated controls and the vancomycin-treated group. MRSA was recovered from
               the spleen in 5/7 saline-treated animals but in none of the antibacterial drug-treated animals.
               Following 14 days therapy, 5/8 ceftobiprole-treated rats and 6/8 vancomycin-treated rats cleared
               MRSA from the sternum compared with none of the saline-treated animals. In those animals that
               did not clear MRSA, only rare colonies were recovered. In rabbits with localized osteomyelitis
               due to MRSA 168-1, ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (40 mg/kg ceftobiprole equivalent, q8h, 4
               weeks) administered subcutaneously was more active than vancomycin (30 mg/kg, q12h, 4
               weeks, subcutaneous) or oral linezolid (60 mg/kg, q8h, 4 weeks) at 2 weeks after end of
               treatment.

               medocaril sodium (equivalent to 4.3 to 34.2 mg/kg of ceftobiprole and concentrations achievable

               200 mg/kg) were administered subcutaneously 1- and 2-hour post-infection (previously shown to

               Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia
               BPR-CS-009 was a randomized, double-blind, multicenter trial conducted to establish the
               efficacy and safety of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium compared to daptomycin in the treatment of
               SAB, including infective endocarditis. The trial assessed microbiological eradication rates
               (negative blood culture for S. aureus) at Day 4, Day 8, and the EOT and PTE visits in the mITT
               population. The mITT population comprised of 387 subjects (ceftobiprole: n = 189; comparator:
               n = 198). In the ceftobiprole group, 74.6% of subjects (141/189) had an MSSA infection at
               baseline, and 23.8% of subjects (45/189) had an MRSA infection at baseline. In the comparator
               group, 73.7% of subjects (146/198) had an MSSA infection, and 24.7% of subjects (49/198) had
               an MRSA infection.

               CABP
               Common typical bacterial pathogens that cause CABP include Streptococcus pneumoniae,
               Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Atypical bacterial
               pathogens such as Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Legionella
               pneumophila also cause CABP. Data from two multiregional phase 3 trials, CAP-3001 and BPR-
               PIP-002 were included to support the CABP indication. Evidence of efficacy and safety in
               HABP from trial BPR 248/307 was included to provide additional information on the pneumonia
               population. The Applicant is not requesting an indication for the treatment of HABP and data
               from this trial were not reviewed for efficacy.

                    19.6. In Vitro Susceptibility Test Method
               The MIC values for ceftobiprole were determined by broth microdilution method in accordance
               with the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines (M07-A6). Tier 1 studies
               evaluated the effect of media (cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton broth, Iso-Sensitest broth), media
               supplementation (25 mg/L calcium, 0.002% Tween 80), temperature (30oC or 35oC), presence of
               2% NaCl, inoculum size, incubation conditions (5%CO2), pH, and serum. A 2-fold increase in
               ceftobiprole MICs against the two P. aeruginosa strains occurred with increase of inoculum
               density from 104 to 105 to 106 CFU/mL Increases in ceftobiprole MIC were also made when high
               inoculum β-lactamase-positive strains were tested. Ceftobiprole MIC values from dry-form broth
               microdilution MIC panels were within 1log2 dilution of the reference frozen-form MIC values.
               Overall, the ceftobiprole MIC obtained under various of testing conditions were within 1log2
               dilution of the standard CLSI broth microdilution method.

               20. Mechanism of Action/Drug Resistance

                    20.1. Mechanism of Action
               Ceftobiprole exerts its antibacterial activity by binding to multiple penicillin-binding proteins
               (PBPs) and inhibiting their transpeptidase activity, which is essential for the synthesis of the
               bacterial cell wall. The concentrations required to inhibit 50% binding to PBPs (IC50s) from
               various gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria were determined using fluorescein-labeled
               penicillin, [H3}-penicillin, biocillin fluorescein-labeled, or fluorescein isothiocyanate labeled
               ampicillin (Table 322 and Table 323). The studies showed that ceftobiprole has a high affinity
               for S. aureus PBPs 1 – 4, including PBP2a in methicillin-resistant S. aureus (Table 322).
               Ceftobiprole has high affinity for all six S. pneumoniae PBPs in penicillin-susceptible strains,
               including PBP2b. Ceftobiprole’s PBP binding affinity is reduced for PBP1b and PBP2b in
               penicillin-resistant strains, but ceftobiprole still has good affinity for PBP1a, PBP2a, PBP2x, and
               PBP3 in these strains. Ceftobiprole has a high affinity for S. epidermidis PBP 2’, compared to all
               other -lactams measured. Ceftobiprole has good affinity for wildtype PBPs 1-5 of E. faecium
               but does not have measurable affinity for the mutated PBP5 from ampicillin-resistant E. faecium,
               resulting in elevated -lactam MICs in E. faecium strains that have these variants of PBP5.

                    20.2. Mechanism of Resistance
               Single-step resistance frequencies were determined for 10 S. aureus strains using agar plates
               containing ceftobiprole at 2x to 8x MIC and an inoculum of 5 x 108 to 5 x 109 CFU. Resistance
               frequencies observed for ceftobiprole were low in S. aureus and ranged from ~9.6 x 10-8 at 2x
               MIC to <1.5 x 10-10 at 8X MIC (Table 326). In serial passage studies, a 4-fold increase in MIC
               was observed in 3 out of 5 S. aureus isolates after 50 passages. In the case of coagulase negative

               staphylococci, the ceftobiprole resistance frequencies were 1.1 x 10-8 to <7.7 x 10-10 and 4 of the
               5 strains had a 4-fold increase in MIC after 50 passages. In most cases, the transiently elevated
               ceftobiprole MICs decreased when the strains were cultured in the absence of drug, suggesting
               the resistance mutations were not stable.
               When a high inoculum of S. aureus strains (109 CFU/mL) was serially passaged in subinhibitory
               concentrations of ceftobiprole for 28 days, resistance due to rare mutations developed in 20-21
               days. For the strain carrying mutated mecA gene on a plasmid with an initial ceftobiprole MIC of
               16 mcg/mL, the MIC increased to 256 mcg/mL after 20 passages. For the strain carrying
               wildtype mecA gene on a plasmid in a mecA– background, ceftobiprole MIC increased from
               4 mcg/mL to 128 mcg/mL after 21 passages. In the third strain that lacked the mecA gene,
               ceftobiprole MIC increased from 1 mcg/mL to 256 mcg/mL after 20 passages. The mecA gene
               acquired mutations which lie close to the ceftobiprole binding site (Banerjee et al. 2008). The
               mutations in the mecA– strain that led to an increased ceftobiprole MIC were in three genes: two
               substitutions were in the gene encoding the low molecular weight PBP4, one in a gene encoding
               a predicted signaling protein, GdpP, and one in the gene encoding an efflux protein, AcrB, which
               is implicated in resistance to cationic compounds.
               Single-step resistance frequencies for ceftobiprole in 10 S. pneumoniae (including penicillin
               sensitive and penicillin resistant) strains ranged from 2 x 10-7 at 2x MIC to <6.7 x 10-9 at 8X
               MIC. Three strains showed a 2-fold increase in MIC after 50 passages.
               Single-step resistance frequencies for ceftobiprole in 8 H. influenzae (including  lactamase
               positive and  lactamase negative) and 2 M. catarrhalis strains resulted in very low resistance
               frequencies of <4.3 x 10-11 to 1.3 x 10-10 at 2x MIC and 8x MIC. A 4-fold increase in MIC was
               seen in one strain after 50 passages.
               Single-step mutants were obtained by exposing clinical isolates of Morganella morganii,
               Citrobacter freundii, Providencia stuartii, Enterobacter cloacae, Serratia marcescens,
               Escherichia coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa to 2x-, 4x- and 8x- ceftobiprole MICs. Single-
               step resistance frequencies for five Enterobacterales strains and one P. aeruginosa strain were
               10-6 to 10-8 at 2x MIC for ceftobiprole and comparable to the values obtained for cefepime and
               ceftazidime. The resistant mutants in C. freundii and E. cloacae occurred at frequencies of 10-6 at
               2x MIC and 4x MIC of ceftobiprole. The mutants appeared to have become resistant through
               over-expression of the chromosomal Class C β-lactamase. Mutants of P. aeruginosa were
               obtained at a frequency of 10-6 and <10-9 at 2x MIC and 4x MIC, respectively. None of the
               mutants over-expressed the chromosomal Class C β-lactamase but were found to over-express
               the MexXY efflux pump (Queenan et al. 2010). The mutation frequencies for Enterobacterales
               and P. aeruginosa were higher than those observed for S. aureus and S. pneumoniae.

               Resistance in Isolates From Ceftobiprole Clinical Trials
               In the CAP-3001 (CABP) trial, K. pneumoniae isolates from 1 subject had a ≥ 4-fold increase in
               the ceftobiprole MICs between baseline (0.12 mcg/mL) and post-baseline (>16 mcg/mL). The
               organism acquired an ESBL (TEM-4 with 4 amino acid changes) (Queenan 2009d). The
               Applicant concluded that ceftobiprole resistance did not develop over the course of therapy and
               the subject was infected with a new strain of K. pneumoniae which had a higher ceftobiprole
               MICs and expressed more resistance mechanisms.
               Subject isolates from the BAP248/307 HABP clinical trial with a ≥4-fold increase in ceftobiprole
               MIC values were characterized by pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (Queenan 2009b). Eleven
               subjects had related or identical isolates post-baseline with increased ceftobiprole MICs analysis.
               All 11 baseline isolates were gram-negative (P. aeruginosa, n=4; A. baumannii, n=2; E. cloacae,
               n = 2; E. coli, n = 1; S. marcescens, n = 1; and K. pneumoniae, n = 1). The pulsed-field gel
               electrophoresis results suggest that resistance to ceftobiprole developed while on therapy for
               these isolates. Subject isolates from the BAP248/307 HABP clinical trial with ceftobiprole MIC
               values ≥16 mcg/mL were evaluated for the expression of β-lactamases. Three principal
               resistance profiles were discovered: (1) ESBL-positive, with CTX-M or SHV family Class A
               extended-spectrum β-lactamases, (2) ESBL-positive, combined with an AmpC Class C β-
               lactamase, (3) ESBL-negative, having an AmpC Class C β-lactamase, either plasmid-encoded or
               chromosomally located. Ceftobiprole is not active against gram-negative bacteria producing
               ESBLs from TEM, SHV or CTX-M families, serine carbapenemases (such as KPC), class B
               metallo-β-lactamases, or class C (AmpC cephalosporinases) expressed at high levels and Ambler
               class D β-lactamases including carbapenemases.
               In summary, resistance in some bacteria is due to poor binding to PBPs, expression of 
               lactamases including AmpC  lactamases, and expression of efflux pumps. In E. faecium, β-
               lactam resistance is mediated by low affinity binding to PBP5, which may be expressed at higher
               levels in ampicillin-resistant isolates. Ceftobiprole is resistant to hydrolysis by S. aureus
               penicillinases and is hydrolyzed slowly by some Class C and Class A β-lactamases found in
               gram- negative bacteria. Like most cephalosporins, ceftobiprole is hydrolyzed by ESBLs, serine
               carbapenemases and metallo-β-lactamases. It is also hydrolyzed by the Class A
               cephalosporinases from Proteus vulgaris, which has inherent resistance to ceftobiprole.

               Cross-Resistance
               Analysis of drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus subset of the 2016-2020 SENTRY surveillance
               isolates demonstrated that ceftobiprole was active against isolates non-susceptible to
               clindamycin, daptomycin, erythromycin, gentamicin, levofloxacin, linezolid,
               tetracycline, tigecycline, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (ceftobiprole susceptibility ranged
               from 97.7%–100.0% based on the proposed ceftobiprole breakpoint of S ≤2 mcg/mL for
               S. aureus). Ceftobiprole MIC50/90 values (e.g., 0.5/2 mcg/mL) were identical for the S. aureus
               subsets with vancomycin MIC values of ≤1 mcg/mL and >1 mcg/mL. Ceftobiprole maintained
               activity against 88.0% of the ceftaroline non-susceptible isolates.

               I. Executive Summary

               1. Overview

                  1.1. Summary of Regulatory Action
               Resmetirom, (trade name REZDIFFRA) is being approved as a thyroid hormone receptor beta
               (THR-beta) agonist indicated in conjunction with diet and exercise for the treatment of adults
               with noncirrhotic nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) with moderate to advanced liver fibrosis
               (consistent with stages F2 to F3 fibrosis). The approved dosage is 80 mg orally once daily (for
               patients weighing less than 100 kg) or 100 mg orally once daily (for patients weighing 100 kg or
               more), with or without food. The approved indication and dosage are different from those
               initially proposed by the Applicant but were agreed upon during the NDA review. The NDA was
               reviewed by the multidisciplinary review team whose reviews and recommendations are reflected in
               this integrated review. Each discipline recommends approval, and the signatory authority for this
               application concurs with those recommendations.
               Substantial evidence of effectiveness for resmetirom in patients with NASH was established
               using data from one adequate and well-controlled trial with confirmatory evidence (CE). Trial
               MGL-3196-11 is the single adequate and well-controlled investigation supporting the
               effectiveness of resmetirom. Both 80 and 100 mg dose arms demonstrated statistical significance
               on prespecified histologic endpoints as surrogate endpoints to support an accelerated approval.
               These results, based on prespecified 52-week liver biopsy endpoints, were persuasive.
               Confirmatory evidence includes MGL-3196-05, a phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
               that enrolled adult patients with noncirrhotic biopsy-proven NASH, who were randomized 2:1 to
               resmetirom 80 mg (n=84) or placebo (n=41). The primary endpoint was the percent change in
               hepatic fat fraction by MRI-PDFF at 12 weeks, with 36-week liver biopsy and MRI-PDFF as
               secondary endpoints. Treatment with resmetirom reduced hepatic fat fraction at 12 and 36 weeks
               and was associated with improved NASH activity scores, higher rates of NASH resolution, and
               reduction of fibrosis stage compared to treatment with placebo.
               This indication will be approved under accelerated approval based on improvement of NASH
               and fibrosis. Continued approval for this indication will be contingent upon verification and
               description of clinical benefit in confirmatory trials. Specifically, Trial MGL-3196-11 continues
               to enroll additional subjects for a total of approximately 1700 subjects. All subjects will be
               followed for up to 54 months to assess clinical outcomes: a composite clinical endpoint of
               progression to cirrhosis, liver decompensation events, liver transplant, and all-cause mortality.
               The available safety data show that resmetirom is safe for its intended use. Common adverse
               reactions include gastrointestinal events (diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, constipation, abdominal
               pain), pruritus and dizziness. Rare, serious adverse reactions include gallbladder-related adverse
               reactions (cholecystitis or gallstone pancreatitis) and drug induced liver injury (DILI). The DILI
               was determined to be most consistent with drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis phenotype
               (DI-ALH), including one observed case meeting Hy’s Law criteria which spontaneously resolved

                  1.2. Conclusions on Substantial Evidence of
                      Effectiveness
               Substantial evidence of effectiveness was established with one adequate and well-controlled
               clinical investigation and confirmatory evidence.
               Substantial evidence of effectiveness for resmetirom in patients with NASH was established
               using data from one adequate and well-controlled trial, MGL-3196-11, with confirmatory
               evidence (CE). Trial MGL-3196-11 is the single adequate and well-controlled investigation
               supporting the effectiveness of resmetirom. The efficacy of resmetirom was evaluated based on
               an prespecified interim analysis at Month 12 of Trial MGL-3196-11, a 54-month, randomized,
               double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Enrolled subjects had metabolic risk factors and a baseline
               or recent liver biopsy showing NASH with fibrosis stage 2 or 3 and a NAFLD Activity Score
               (NAS) of at least 4.
               Efficacy determination was based on the effect of resmetirom on 1) the percentage of patients
               with resolution of steatohepatitis and no worsening of liver fibrosis and 2) the percentage of
               patients with at least one stage improvement in liver fibrosis and no worsening of steatohepatitis.
               The Month 12 analysis included 888 F2 and F3 subjects randomized 1:1:1 to receive placebo (n
               = 294), resmetirom 80 mg once daily (n = 298), or resmetirom 100 mg once daily (n = 296), in
               addition to lifestyle counseling on nutrition and exercise. Patients were on stable doses of
               medications for diabetes, dyslipidemia, and hypertension.
               Two pathologists, Pathologist A and Pathologist B, independently read the liver biopsies for each
               patient. Both the 80 mg once daily and the 100 mg once daily dosages of resmetirom
               demonstrated improvement on both histopathology endpoints at Month 12 compared to placebo.

                  2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
               Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) with moderate to advanced liver fibrosis (consistent with
               stage F2 and F3) is a common condition, which can be progressive—on average, patients with
               NASH progress one fibrosis stage every 7 years. NASH prevalence has increased worldwide,
               and there are currently no approved pharmacologic therapies that have been shown to reduce
               steatohepatitis and/or fibrosis.
               Resmetirom, a first-in-class new molecular entity, is a partial agonist of the thyroid hormone
               receptor β. In the pivotal trial (MGL-3196-11) reviewed to support efficacy, after one year of
               treatment, the population had statistically significant improvements in liver histology, both for
               steatohepatitis and fibrosis. These data were sufficiently persuasive for accelerated approval of
               resmetirom on the basis of a single adequate and well-controlled trial plus confirmatory
               evidence. Completion of the pivotal trial, including assessment of clinically meaningful
               endpoints that demonstrate progression of liver disease is of critical importance, to ensure that
               histologic improvement is accompanied by clinically meaningful benefit as well as to evaluate
               long-term safety. The 54-month assessment also may elucidate whether resmetirom treatment
               over a longer period is required to reverse fibrosis and/or steatohepatitis, and whether long term
               treatment has a clinically meaningful benefit on preventing progression to cirrhosis or hepatic
               decompensation events, including death and need for liver transplant.
               The Applicant enrolled participants who had NASH with stages F1, F2, and F3 fibrosis, but the
               primary analysis and the indicated population is patients with NASH with moderate to advanced
               liver fibrosis, consistent with stage F2 and F3. Progression to cirrhosis and other clinically
               meaningful liver endpoints in patients with lower stages of fibrosis (F0 and F1) is too slow and
               indolent to be able to demonstrate benefits in the context of a clinical trial and would require a
               greater assurance of safety to support a favorable benefit:risk assessment for long-term use. , An
               evaluation of the drug in patients with F4 fibrosis (cirrhosis) is ongoing.
               Safety data were reviewed from the pivotal trial along with an additional placebo-controlled,
               randomized safety study. This safety database was adequate. Serious adverse events were similar
               across treatment arms. The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal, including
               diarrhea and nausea, which were also the most common causes of treatment discontinuation.
               Based on the mechanism of action, thyroid function testing laboratory and clinical data were
               carefully reviewed, and clinically significant abnormalities in thyroid function were not detected.
               Although one case of probable drug-induced liver injury met Hy’s law, this case resolved with
               drug discontinuation without further intervention. Elevated autoimmune markers and
               immunoglobulin G suggested a drug induced autoimmune hepatitis like injury, which is more
               likely to respond to treatment (e.g., corticosteroids) than other types of idiosyncratic drug-
               induced liver injury, if the injury does not spontaneously resolve with drug discontinuation.
               Adopting an enhanced pharmacovigilance strategy for the first 2 years after approval will
               expedite reporting of any additional hepatotoxicity cases for Agency review.
               Based on review of all available efficacy and safety data, the benefits of resmetirom outweigh
               the risks of treatment in adult NASH patients with moderate to advanced liver fibrosis to support
               an accelerated approval based on improvement of NASH and fibrosis. Continued approval for

               II. Interdisciplinary Assessment

               3. Introduction
               This review serves as the interdisciplinary assessment for REZDIFFRA (NDA 217785),
               submitted for approval under the accelerated approval pathway (subpart H) based on a surrogate
               endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. REZDIFFRA contains resmetirom, which,
               as proposed by the Applicant, is indicated for treatment of adults with nonalcoholic
               steatohepatitis (NASH) with liver fibrosis.

               Analysis of Condition
               NASH is a severe form of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). NAFLD is characterized by
               the presence of macrovesicular steatosis in ≥5% of hepatocytes and includes a spectrum of
               disease from bland steatosis (nonalcoholic fatty liver or NAFL) to more severe forms, i.e.,
               NASH with stage 3 liver fibrosis, and in a proportion of patients may progress to cirrhosis.
               NAFLD is a diagnosis of exclusion, as other causes of steatosis, including but not limited to
               medications, starvation, or monogenic disorders, must be excluded in individuals who have little
               or no alcohol consumption (defined as <20 g/d for women and <30 g/d for men). NASH is
               characterized by the presence of steatosis, inflammatory changes, and ballooning degeneration of
               hepatocytes, with or without fibrosis (Rinella et al. 2023b).
               The prevalence of NAFLD and NASH is rising worldwide, paralleling the increases in the
               prevalence of obesity and metabolic comorbid disease. The prevalence of NAFLD in adults is
               estimated to be between 25 to 30% of the general population. NASH prevalence in the general
               population is difficult to estimate, given the need for histological confirmation. Historically,
               reported prevalence estimates for NASH range from 1.5% to 6.45%, but in one recent study
               NASH was identified in 14% of asymptomatic patients undergoing colon cancer screening,
               suggesting an increase in prevalence of NASH. NAFLD and NASH incidence data from the
               general population is lacking, but it has been estimated that the incidence of NAFLD ranges from
               28.01 per 1000 person‐years (PY) (95% CI: 19.34, 40.57) to 52.34 per 1000 PY (95% CI: 28.31,
               96.77) (Younossi 2018; Hamid et al. 2022; Rinella et al. 2023b). There are differences in
               prevalence between racial and ethnic subpopulations, with the highest prevalence in Americans
               of Hispanic/Latino descent, followed by white Americans, and Black/African Americans
               (Sayiner et al. 2016).
               There is a bidirectional association between NAFLD and metabolic abnormalities (central
               obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and hypertension) wherein NAFLD can often precede
               development of metabolic abnormalities, and having several metabolic abnormalities increases
               the risk of histological progression of NASH (Rinella et al. 2023b). The presence and severity of
               obesity are associated with NAFLD and progression of disease. In fact, 90% of morbidly obese
               persons have NAFLD and the prevalence of NASH among obese individuals is estimated to be
               25% to 30%. Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus are at the greatest risk for NAFLD and
               NASH. The prevalence of NASH among the patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus is estimated to
               be as high as 65%.

               Though NAFLD and NASH are more common in obese individuals, NAFLD and NASH can
               occur in the absence of obesity. The prevalence of NAFLD in lean individuals in the United
               States is estimated to be about 7%, compared to prevalence in Asian countries, where it can be as
               high as 25% to 30% (Younossi 2018; Younossi and Henry 2022; Rinella et al. 2023b).
               The degree of fibrosis has been linked to development of liver-related outcomes and death.
               Patients with stage 2 fibrosis and higher are at increased risk for all-cause mortality (Rinella et
               al. 2023b). Progression of fibrosis is associated with a higher likelihood of liver-related events.
               (Angulo et al. 2015; Ekstedt et al. 2015; Sanyal et al. 2021). The rate of fibrosis progression is
               higher in patients with NASH (one stage per 7 years) compared to those with NAFL (one stage
               per 14 years) (Singh et al. 2015).
               From a natural history perspective, NAFL is generally considered as a benign condition, whereas
               NASH is considered a progressive disease that can advance to cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation,
               hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), liver transplantation, or death. Approximately 10 to 15% of
               NASH patients will progress to cirrhosis, but this progression is nonlinear and some patients
               with NASH fibrosis may spontaneously regress (Younossi 2018). Progression to cirrhosis places
               NASH patients at high risk for developing decompensated cirrhosis (variceal bleeding, hepatic
               encephalopathy, ascites). Among patients with cirrhosis, progression to clinical decompensation
               ranges from 3% to 20% per year. HCC as a complication of NASH is the second most common
               indication for HCC-related liver transplantation, after hepatitis C-associated HCC. NASH is the
               second most common indication for listing for liver transplantation and the leading indication for
               liver transplant among women in the United States (Younossi and Henry 2022). The most
               common causes of death in NAFLD are cardiovascular disease and nonhepatic malignancy,
               followed by liver disease (Rinella et al. 2023b).

               Current Treatment Options
               There are currently no FDA-approved pharmacological treatments for NASH. Lifestyle
               management with reduced calorie diet and increased exercise are currently considered the
               standard of care. Bariatric surgery as a therapeutic option can be considered in patients who meet
               criteria for metabolic weight loss surgery as it can resolve NAFLD or NASH in the majority of
               patients without cirrhosis. NASH resolution was seen in 80% of patients 1 year following
               surgery and was maintained at 5 years. However, bariatric surgery is a high-risk procedure with a
               risk of surgical complications. It is not recommended in NASH patients with cirrhosis and is
               contraindicated in patients who have decompensated cirrhosis from any cause. Glucagon-like
               peptide 1 agonists like semaglutide can be considered for their approved indications (type 2
               diabetes mellitus/obesity) in patients with concomitant NASH for their cardiovascular and
               metabolic benefits, but no glucagon-like peptide 1 agonist is approved for the treatment of
               NASH. Other medications used off label include vitamin E and pioglitazone, but these have not
               demonstrated an antifibrotic benefit (Rinella et al. 2023b).
               Therefore, pharmacological treatment for NASH remains an unmet medical need.

               Resmetirom
               Resmetirom, a new molecular entity (NME), is a partial agonist of the thyroid hormone receptor
               β (THR­β). See Section 5.2 for details on mechanism of action (MOA). The Applicant has

               Rationale for Thyroid Hormone Receptor β Agonism
               Lipotoxicity is a key driver in the pathogenesis of NASH, driven by excess free fatty acids
               coupled with increased de novo lipogenesis. Thyroid hormones (THs) regulate hepatic lipid
               metabolism. In experimental studies, mice fed a Western diet developed increased steatosis,
               inflammation, and fibrosis, and subsequently demonstrated decreased intrahepatic
               tetraiodothyronine (T4), and triiodothyronine (T3). In a dietary mouse model of NASH, THs
               decreased hepatic triglyceride content and hydroxyproline. Thyroid hormones also restored
               autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis to increase β­oxidation of fatty acids, and reduced
               lipotoxicity, oxidative stress, hepatic inflammation, and fibrosis (Bruinstroop et al. 2021; Zhou et
               al. 2022).
               Despite the known role of THs in regulation of hepatic lipid metabolism, the association between
               hypothyroidism and NAFLD from an epidemiological perspective remains unclear. In a large
               meta-analysis, hypothyroidism was significantly associated with presence and severity of
               NAFLD, whereas in another meta-analysis, no association between NAFLD and hypothyroidism
               was noted, along with no difference between TH levels between subjects with or without
               NAFLD (Jaruvongvanich et al. 2017; Mantovani et al. 2018).
               The two main forms of THs—T3, the active form of TH, and T4, a prohormone activated by
               deiodinases at the cellular and circulatory level—exert their actions via the thyroid hormone
               receptor (THR), which is primarily a nuclear receptor that acts as a ligand-dependent
               transcription factor. There are two major THR genes, THRA and THRB. THR­α1 and THR­α2
               are two major THRA receptor splice variants encoded by the THRA gene, whereas THR­β1and
               THR­β2 are two major THRB isoforms generated by alternate promoter choice on the THRB
               gene. THR­α1 is highly expressed in the heart, bone, and skeletal muscle, whereas THR­α2 is
               widely expressed throughout the whole body. THR­β1 is predominately expressed in the brain,
               liver, and kidney, whereas THR­β2 is found in the pituitary, retina, and cochlea (Singh and Yen
               2017). Thyroid hormone receptor α (THR­α) has also been found in hepatic stellate cells. Thus,
               increased T3 and T4 levels could induce profibrogenic effects by activation of stellate cells
               (Ritter et al. 2020; Hatziagelaki et al. 2022).
               The THR­β pathway regulates de novo lipogenesis, β­oxidation of fatty acids, mitophagy,
               mitochondrial oxidation, and cholesterol synthesis. In animal studies, hepatomegaly and hepatic
               steatosis were noted in mice with dominant negative mutations in the gene encoding THR­β,
               secondary to decreased THR-mediated fatty acid β­oxidation, which leads to lipid accumulation
               (Sinha et al. 2018). Given that THR­β is highly expressed in the liver, there is significant interest
               in development of THR analogs that can separate the beneficial actions on the liver mediated by
               THR­β (reduction of triglycerides and cholesterol) from the harmful actions on heart and bone,
               mediated by THR­α.)
               In nonclinical studies, resmetirom demonstrated a stronger activation of THR­β compared to
               THR­α. It also showed rapid and robust lowering of non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol,

               Brief Regulatory History
               See Section 12 for a full summary of the regulatory history.
               An IND application for resmetirom for the treatment of NASH was opened on July 25, 2016, and
               the IND-opening study was deemed safe to proceed on August 24, 2016. Fast Track Designation
               was granted to resmetirom on October 18, 2019, based on phase 2 trial (MGL-3196-05) results,
               which demonstrated reduction in hepatic fat fraction as measured by magnetic resonance
               imaging-proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF). On April 11, 2023, resmetirom was granted
               breakthrough designation based on preliminary efficacy data obtained from Trial MGL-3196-11
               (phase 3 pivotal trial), and on May 22, 2023, the Applicant was granted rolling review.

               Change in Nomenclature for NAFLD/NASH
               An international Delphi consensus process led to revised nomenclature for NAFLD and NASH
               which was introduced in 2023. The proposed nomenclature for NAFLD is metabolic
               dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). MASLD is diagnosed if a patient has
               hepatic steatosis (>5% hepatocytes) with at least one cardiometabolic risk factor. Screening for
               other potential causes of steatotic liver disease is still indicated. The new nomenclature for
               NASH is metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) with no change in
               histopathological criteria. The FDA considers the terms NAFLD and NASH, interchangeable
               with MASLD and MASH, respectively (December 2018; Rinella et al. 2023a).
               The FDA has maintained the former nomenclature for NASH in this review and labeling. Most
               non-hepatology clinicians may be unfamiliar with the new nomenclature, and it is too early to
               know whether there will be universal acceptance of this new nomenclature. Additionally, the
               term NASH was used in the regulatory designations for the IND and NDA for resmetirom, i.e.,
               fast track, breakthrough therapy designation, and priority review.

                        3.1.2. Key Safety Review Issues

                         3.1.2.1. Hepatotoxicity: Drug-Induced Liver Injury
               Resmetirom is a thyromimetic, partial agonist of THR­β, with actions on the hepatocyte
               purported to provide beneficial metabolic effects on reducing lipotoxicity, primarily through
               action on THR­β, the predominant hepatocyte THR. However, resmetirom also has some action
               on THR­α (see Section 5.2). Thyromimetics are associated with safety signals related to the liver.
               In the pooled trial safety database (Trials MGL-3196-11 and MGL-3196-14), there were 10
               potential Hy’s law cases in both drug arms, but after detailed review, only one case of probable
               drug-induced liver injury (DILI) was observed. Refer to Section 7.7.1 for the full analysis of this
               key safety review issue.

                         3.1.2.2. Treatment-Related Changes in Thyroid Hormones
               Resmetirom is intended to act in the liver while avoiding unwanted systemic actions of TH in
               heart and bone mediated through THR­α. Although a THR- ß agonist, resmetirom does have
               some agonist activity on THR­α receptors (see Section 5.2), therefore may have potential effects
               on the TH axis. Refer to Section 7.7.2 for the full analysis of this key safety review issue.

                        3.1.2.3. Treatment-Related Gallstone Adverse Events
               There is a strong association between gallstone disease and NAFLD/NASH. Because resmetirom
               is a thyromimetic compound, targeting hepatic THR-ß, it is expected to promote bile formation
               and secretion, increase cholesterol metabolism, formation of bile acids, and increase secretion of
               cholesterol, increasing the potential for gallstone formation. Refer to Section 7.7.3 for the full
               analysis of this key safety review issue.

                        3.1.2.4. Treatment-Related Gastrointestinal Adverse Events
               Gastrointestinal (GI) AEs were the most common treatment-emergent adverse event (TEAE)
               reported during the development program. Refer to Section 7.7.4 for the full analysis of this key
               safety review issue.

                        3.1.2.5. Treatment-Related Pruritus
               Although pruritus has not been considered a common problem for patients with NASH, NASH
               with advanced fibrosis (F3/F4) can be associated with clinically significant pruritus. Pruritus has
               been found to be a TEAE in clinical trials evaluating other potential therapies for NASH, such as
               FXR agonists. Refer to Section 7.7.5 for the full analysis of this key safety review issue.

                        3.1.2.6. Deficiencies in the Pre- and Postnatal Development
                                Study in Rats
               The PPND study in rats is deficient based on current ICH standards. Refer to Section 7.7.6 for
               the full analysis of this key safety review issue.

                        3.1.2.7. Treatment-Related Changes in Sex Hormones
               The impact of changes in sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) and associated sex hormones
               (including estradiol, testosterone, FSH, and LH) in the setting of pharmacological intervention
               for NASH was unknown. Refer to Section 7.7.7 for the full analysis of this key safety review
               issue.

                        3.1.2.8. Treatment-Related Changes in Bone Metabolism
               Resmetirom is a THR-ß partial agonist with high selectivity for hepatic THR-ß. However,
               potential off-target adverse effects of resmetirom via THR­α agonism may affect bone
               metabolism. Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) also has direct action on bone. Refer to Section
               7.7.8 for the full analysis of this key safety review issue.

                        3.1.2.9. Major Cardiovascular Events
               Even though resmetirom is a partial THR-ß agonist, no thyromimetic is a pure THR­β or THR­α
               agonist. Therefore, there is a possibility of off-target effects, which include cardiotoxicity as the

                        3.1.2.10. Malignancy
               Patients with NASH are at increased risk of malignancies, including HCC. Comorbid obesity

                   3.2. Approach to the Clinical Review
               For this submission, the review team assessed efficacy from Trial MGL-3196-11, the pivotal trial
               in adult patients with biopsy-proven NASH with fibrosis. The efficacy analysis, evaluating both
               resmetirom doses (80 mg and 100 mg) compared to placebo, was performed for subjects with
               stage F2 and F3 fibrosis at baseline (Section 6.2).
               The primary safety analysis was conducted using data from Trials MGL-3196-11 and MGL-
               3196-14, including all subjects receiving placebo or resmetirom at 80 mg or 100 mg. The safety
               data from Trials MGL-3196-18 and MGL-3196-05 were also reviewed to support the primary
               safety analysis but are not described in detail in this review.

               5. Pharmacologic Activity, Pharmacokinetics,
                   and Clinical Pharmacology

                   5.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential
                       Effectiveness
               The potential effectiveness of resmetirom was tested in vitro (cell-free functional assay) and in
               vivo (mouse model). The dataset did not include any in vivo models that produced all the
               histological features of NASH (i.e., steatosis, inflammation, hepatocyte ballooning, and fibrosis).
               However, from a nonclinical perspective, the data are considered as adequate for supporting
               approval from pharmacology/toxicology perspective. In summary:
               •    In the THR­β cell-free functional assay performed by the Applicant, the half maximal
                    effective concentration (EC50) value for resmetirom was 0.70µM (see details in Section 13.2).
                    The published EC50 value for resmetirom for the same assay was 0.21 µM. The published
                    EC50 value is included in Section 12.1 of the label.
               •    In the THR­α cell-free functional assay performed by the Applicant, the EC50 value for
                    resmetirom was 3.83µM (see details in Section 13.2). The published EC50 value for
                    resmetirom for the same assay was 3.74uM. The published EC50 value is included in Section
                    12.1 of the label.
               •    The potency of resmetirom in the THR­β cell-free functional assay was 17.8 times the
                    potency for THR­α activation based on the published EC50 values, and 5.5 times the potency
                    for THR­α activation based on the EC50 values from the same assay performed independently
                    by the Applicant.
               •    Decreases in liver weight and severity of liver vacuolation were observed in mice fed an
                    admixture of resmetirom (RO4923659) and high-fat diet (HFD) for 25 weeks compared to
                    placebo+HFD admixture-fed control animals. In liver, transcripts for some inflammatory
                    genes and major fibrosis-associated genes were downregulated in resmetirom+HFD
                    admixture-fed animals to levels that were similar to those measured in normal control
                    animals. Resmetirom administration had the expected effects on THR-regulated genes
                    (mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, malic enzyme, deiodinase 1, thyroid
                    binding globulin) in the liver.
               •    Established pharmacologic class (EPC): Resmetirom is a first-in-class NME. The
                    recommended EPC for resmetirom is thyroid hormone receptor-beta (THR-β) agonist. The
                    review team agrees that the selected EPC meets the criteria of being scientifically valid and
                    clinically meaningful, in accordance with the FDA guidance for industry, Labeling for
                    Human Prescription Drug and Biological Products—Determining Established
                    Pharmacologic Class for Use in the Highlights of Prescribing Information (October 2009).
                    The recommended EPC differs slightly from the EPC proposed by the Applicant, thyroid
                    hormone receptor beta (THR-β) selective agonist.

               MGL-3196 (resmetirom) and the major human metabolite MGL-3623 were evaluated in a cell-

               to bind to the THR-retinoid X receptor (RXR) heterodimer complex, which mediates TH
               signaling. The functional assay measured the ability of MGL-3196, MGL-3623, or T3 to
